We have conducted an in-depth examination of the interactions between a quantum dot and a superconducting terminal under the influence of charge sensing and dynamic gate technology. The evolution of the quantum dot's charge state over time following a quench is monitored and recorded in three different scenarios: (1) when the quantum dot does not have a excess charge, (2) when the quantum dot carries a single unit of excess charge, and (3) when the quantum dot is in close proximity to the superconducting terminal with no excess charge. By comparing these scenarios to theoretical models, we are able to accurately describe the dot's charge dynamics as it undergoes a quench and find that it closely aligns with a model that accounts for common-coincidence events. Furthermore, our findings suggest that for scenario (3), the Cooper-pair tunneling rate is significantly lower than what would be predicted based on the diffusion of particles alone. As a result, this approach can be utilized to investigate a wide variety of different interaction mechanisms between quantum dots and superconducting terminals that have not yet been explored.

This research provides the necessary criteria for obtaining entropy contractions from suitable metrics on data spaces of conservation laws, specifically for various types of conservation law systems and frameworks. We establish specific standards for obtaining entropy contractions in several contexts, such as for a single conservation law, systems of conservation laws, dependent parameters, dependent variables with their values determined by an ODE, and for a general framework. The standards established for these scenarios are all similar and straightforward, and can be easily applied. The research also proves that any conservation law system or framework meeting the specified criteria naturally satisfies an Lp contraction estimate, and that an Lp contraction estimate for the semigroup generated by a conservation law system or framework implies the existence of an entropy contraction under certain conditions on p and q.

The task of view generation involves creating new images from given single views. We investigate this task using a conditional diffusion model combined with a generator network trained from real-world images. We introduce a dynamic feature extractor that retains information about object orientations during the process. This approach produces high-quality, realistic images with accurate spatial and orientation properties compared to existing methods. Compared to state-of-the-art models, our system demonstrates superior performance in both image quality and perceptual metrics.

A data-driven approach is taken to predict and improve the performance of complex systems, such as disease spread, by using time-series data from a few strategically selected locations. A novel neural network model is introduced that operates without system representation or knowledge, relying solely on input-output data. This model, built using long short-term memory, is able to learn and replicate the connections between different systems, enabling its use on unsupervised and semi-supervised problems. When applied to a model of interconnected populations, the model effectively predicts the transmission dynamics, identifies the most influential locations, and finds the most effective solutions to control the spread. It successfully replaces a complex model of disease transmission with a simple, portable, and unsupervised machine learning model that can be used on a computer with limited resources.

The stability of a liquid layer bound to a fibre is examined when subjected to a force that lowers the layer's Newtonian viscosity, using a parameter that increases with the applied tension. This instability is similar to the Rayleigh-Plateau instability and is influenced by two factors: the layer's thickness and the viscosity of the liquid. The study finds that as the applied tension increases, areas of the layer with decreased viscosity first experience the Rayleigh-Plateau instability, causing the liquid to bulge out at the fibre ends before finally failing at the centre of the layer. The study provides calculations to determine the relationship between tension, viscosity, and bulging sizes. The findings are relevant to several liquids, such as polymer melts and bio-polymers, whose viscosity is affected by tension and may exhibit non-Newtonian behavior when subjected to high levels of stress.

The Hunter-Saxton equation holds significant importance as a geometric flow that realizes the Nijenhuis rotation minimization. This equation appears in a variety of contexts, including symmetry reductions of the 40-point Euler-Poincare system, supergeodesics within the \(\mathfrak{so}(2,1)\) simple Lie algebra, and also in kadomtsev-petviashvili type equations. Certain properties of the equation have already been investigated; however, the discussion on \(\mathfrak{so}(2,1)\) supergeodesics raises questions about the Lipschitz stability of solutions. This paper explores this concept on the HS formula solutions, revealing that local Lipschitz stability applies. Moreover, a broader definition of Lipschitz continuity is also discussed, utilizing the Birkhoff-Klein approach via area and Carathéodory metrics for geometric flows.

A recently developed robotic technology enables automated ultrasound (US) imaging, 
allowing for increased precision and reduced variability in US measurement readings.
This novel approach was tested by assessing and comparing the scoliosis 
severity measured through robotic and manual imaging techniques under the same 
US probe. Eight healthy scoliosis patients participated in the study, with 
scoliosis curves ranging from 40 to 80 degrees. Two experienced US operators 
measured and recorded the lateral and anterior spinal ishpestris angle measurements 
using both robotic and manual methods. These results were subsequently evaluated 
using US mean and median values for consistency and reliability. The study's 
findings revealed strong agreement between the two measurement methods, with 
robust scolionetric parameters observed across both robotic and manual scans. 
Furthermore, both methods yielded reliable data with consistent coefficients 
of variation. Given the accuracy and reliability of robotic imaging, it has been 
considered a viable replacement for traditional manual scanning in the evaluation 
of scoliosis through US imaging.

This paper introduces a novel approach to creating extended or condensed speech segments while maintaining natural-sounding prosody, using a median-based method. Unlike previous techniques that alter speech duration based on the prosody of surrounding sounds, the proposed method generates new speech lengths by modifying the median tempo. A specific strategy for finding this median tempo is developed and differentiation is made regarding its application to speech segments of varying lengths. Moreover, the technique is incorporated into a prior method that adjusts speech tempo to create more natural-sounding prosody and is demonstrated to be effective at producing robust, median-driven extended or condensed speech. Several metrics, including listening tests, PCC, RMSE, and L2 distance, are employed to evaluate the generated speech. Moreover, the technique is found to be effective across a range of speech lengths and there is little audible difference between the original and modified speech.

This paper suggests a novel approach to detecting hate speech that leverages
word embeddings. We investigate the efficacy of combining word and character
embeddings from BERT and XLM models in identifying hate content. Our model
achieves performance enhancements by utilizing both representations. The
results of this study indicate that character-based models offer hate speech
detection advantages that are difficult for word-based models to match.

Multi-input multi-output (MIMO) models excel in their ability to handle complex image classifications and object detection tasks, achieving this through the integration of multiple models where each model processes a portion of the image. However, current approaches suffer from a flaw where each sub-model tries to optimize the information extracted from the image, rather than working together to share and capitalize on their strengths and create a more comprehensive understanding of the image. In order to rectify this issue, we are proposing novel training and modification techniques for MIMO frameworks, where the goal is for each sub-model to learn distinct features and have them work together to create a more complete and unified image representation. This is achieved by introducing a shared feature fusion mechanism that combines the features extracted by the sub-models into a unified representation, resulting in an image-rich feature set that is then used for classification tasks. Additionally, we are also proposing a unique mechanism where the feature features learned by one sub-model are shared and utilized by other sub-models, resulting in an overall increase in performance. Our techniques have been tested and validated on multiple tasks including image classification and object detection, resulting in substantial gains in performance.

This study offers a comprehensive review of prominent datasets containing historical documents, focusing on the progression of techniques employed for image identification and the diverse applications of dataset analyses within both social science research and everyday life.

This study aims to improve joint control in industrial robots using Cartesian continuity. It's worth noting that end-effector smoothness is crucial, but conventional methods prioritize joint continuity instead. This research proposes a smoothness-based control strategy that prioritizes Cartesian continuity for the first time. A theoretical model based on the Denavit-Hartenberg parameters is developed to achieve this goal, and the proposed method is compared to the existing approach in terms of smoothness. A PID controller is combined with the new smoothness-based control to demonstrate its effectiveness, using an actual robot arm and a virtual environment to test the results.

This work incorporates multiple examination phases and multidimensional approaches into the analysis of a cumulative distribution functions for multiple time-to-event data. These enhancements cover key aspects of a distribution function, specifically the infinitesimal and large-scale behavior. The large-scale behavior is relevant in the context of long-term health outcomes, particularly observing a second myocardial infarction. Theoretical distributions with multidimensional characteristics are analyzed and compared with empirical data from a study. The examination of mean and variance behavior in the multidimensional context sheds light on how these parameters relate to each other. A smooth distribution function in the multidimensional context reveals patterns of early and late transition probabilities between states, offering a more detailed examination than one-dimensional time-to-event data. The results from a statistical model based on a parametric distribution in the multidimensional context confirm risk factors for myocardial infarction, consistent with existing knowledge. The implications of this research are relevant to a broader population with health issues.

In the theoretical treatment of chemical reactions, where the potential energy surface can be modeled, a quadrature approach is typically employed to divide the surface into separate sections. Each segment, evaluated independently, approximates the energy associated with its area of influence. This method has been widely used in approaches such as the Metropolis algorithm and Monte Carlo simulations. When dealing with multiple research sites collaborating on a large-scale calculation, a quadrium that can be adapted is necessary. However, previous efforts to develop flexible quadratures were limited in their application, often unable to handle multi-site arrangements. A new quadrature method, designed for efficient and flexible use in a variety of settings and scales, is presented in this study, which successfully achieves a smooth transition while adhering to the requirements of microscopic reversibility. The proposed approach is compatible with a range of path ensemble simulations and has a growing number of degrees of freedom. To validate its efficacy, the study compared the newly developed quadrature with existing models when applied to a simple harmonic oscillator and a triatomic molecule model. The results demonstrate that this method offers a significant improvement in adaptability and efficiency while maintaining a high level of accuracy.

A connected, undirected graph G is deemed weakly resolved with respect to a set of vertices R if each element of R has a distinct minimum path length to every remaining vertex. A resolution verifying subset of G is any set of vertices R such that G is weakly resolved by R. The problem of resolving verification seeks to find the smallest such subset R. A graph's resolution verification dimension (RVD) is the smallest size of the smallest resolving subset R. Initially, RVD was assessed in an unparameterized context and here it is investigated in relation to parameters like the size of the largest feedback clique (fbc) and the largest induced odd- or bipartite subgraph (mco and mbc, respectively). A function f that maps vertices to values and lists of integers describes a pre-paragraph, specifying which components to employ. A graph G is said to possess a pre-paragraph with width w and depth d if every subgraph H of G adheres to the criteria that the number of vertices in H that satisfy a certain condition is less than or equal to the width (w), and the number of vertices not satisfying that condition in H that are at a distance (d) from the violating vertices in H is also less than or estimated by the width (w). This study introduces a topological classification of directed spaces that captures the concept of directed homotopy in a uniform manner. This classification encompasses simple directions, a fundamental characteristic of directed spaces, and yields a two-tiered hierarchy. The upper tier comprises the basic directed homotopy type, encompassing all simple directions, while the lower tier is reserved for more refined types, such as $\mathsf{Rd}_*^1$ and weak simple directions. To achieve this, a new mathematical framework is developed that combines the properties of preorders, directed homotopy types, and monoids. This uniform approach provides a comprehensive understanding of simple directions, weak simple directions, and directed spaces themselves. Furthermore, Sierpinski's cube and the unit circle are employed to demonstrate distinctions between these different levels of refinement.

Planets like Proxima b and TRAPPIST-1 e, located near their respective stars' habitable zones, are subjected to fluctuating atmospheric and surface temperatures. These temperatures fluctuate due to varying levels of insolation and the presence of a thick atmosphere that supports seasonal changes. In the case of TRAPPIST-1 e, a close proximity to its star results in extreme surface temperatures differences between solides and nights, ranging from up to 40 degrees Celsius. In the case of Proxima b, a closer examination of its atmosphere has shown that atmospheric escape significantly impacts its temperature, resulting in a largely molten surface with temperatures around 850 degrees Kelvin during the day and up to 550 degrees Kelvin at night. In an attempt to better understand and predict the surface and atmospheric conditions of exoplanets like TRAPPIST-1 e and Proxima b, researchers have simulated and studied their climate patterns, resulting in a model that accurately replicates a greenhouse climate with molten surface and atmospheric pressure conditions. In this simulated climate model, researchers discovered periodic temperature fluctuations in the surface soil and subsurface, lasting about 7 days, resulting from a predicted thermal relaxation time in the range of 7 to 30 sols, influenced by factors such as surface temperature, atmospheric pressure, and water content. These periodic temperature variations in the surface and subsurface can result in a pattern of dry and saturated areas, potentially affecting water flow and geological activity.

We have developed an approach to construct higher-spin gauge fields with spin greater than one and a half, by building upon self-dual Yang-Mills theories extended into twistor space. This involves introducing twistor creations operators that adhere to conformal symmetry, thereby constraining the resulting gauge fields. These operators split into two categories, one of which gives rise to a linear field with two undetermined components, while the other gives rise to a field with these components separated into spin-one and spin-two parts. By applying the parent operators to various functions, we can construct diverse gauge fields, including those with higher spins up to five and a half, as well as supersymmetric and superconformal versions of these fields. Notably, the supersymmetric construction method works to the loop level, with the result being a supersymmetric expansion of self-dual Yang-Mills theory itself. This approach also offers a new method for defining non-linear spinor multiplets, by applying a twistor creation operator to an arbitrary spinor, with this method providing an alternative to the Regge-Wheeler recipe.

In medical image categorization, using a conventional dataset can be problematic because it often contains inaccurate labels, which can significantly weaken deep learning models' performance when they rely on noisy data. This is particularly concerning since removing the noise is a complex task, especially in situations with limited, high-dimensional data. This study presents an innovative approach called BLRM that utilizes a Bayesian model to continuously refine the labels in an interactive process between a user and a deep learning model. A key component of BLRM is its non-interactive algorithm that helps to identify potentially inaccurate labels and suggests alternative, corrected labels based on the analysis of the training data's statistical properties. BLRM has been applied to two medical datasets, yielding a significant improvement in performance, with an average increase of over 13% in accuracy compared to a baseline model.

Consider a compact set $K$ within the complex plane, and a function space defined by the set of functions that decrease at a specific rate as the distance from $K$ increases, with their norms bounded within the region at a specific distance from $K$. Let this space be denoted as $\mathfrak{L}^p_{\delta,m}(\mathbb{C})$. A linear operator that interpolates functions within a function space defined by the set of functions that decrease at a specific rate, with their norms bounded within the region at a specific distance from $K$, and meets certain estimates is investigated. This operator is found to be bounded from $\mathfrak{L}^p_{\delta,m}(\mathbb{C})$ to $\mathfrak{L}^q_{\delta,m}(\mathbb{C})$ with explicit norm estimates that depend on $\delta$, $m$, and $\zeta$.

Several key concepts in mathematics and computer science, such as Markov chains and matrix computation, rely on the irreducible transition probability matrix, which can be evaluated using a novel, distinct polynomial when the related random walk is connected. This polynomial, whose coefficients are integers, can also determine if a discrete Markov chain is a ergodic system. This makes it a crucial tool for researchers working with finite state Markov chains. This distinction is not observable when employing the standard transition probability matrix's characteristic or transfer matrix. Additionally, an algorithm has been developed that uses this polynomial to identify the largest eigenvalue, an important metric for researchers working with Markov chains, which can also aid in determining the principal eigenvector, a fundamental component in matrix computation.

In this work, we establish a theoretical framework for managing dated events within a logic system, with a specific approach used in the Higher Order Logic of the HOL proof system, where we introduce an element - timed events, allowing for a logic representation and an operation to derive consequences from combined event and time information. A timed event is defined as an association of an event and a point in time, and is divided into past and future timed events. Past events are characterized by having a point in the past, implying they have occurred before, while past happens relationships are redefined to accommodate time, including the notion of being simultaneous in the past. Future events are redefined using the concept of time eligibility, providing the necessary condition for occurring events. Additionally, this concept is applied to events conditioned by time, representing events whose occurrence depends on the passage of time. A rule for deriving conclusions from timed events is also formulated, and its application demonstrated through a set of examples and validation, including recursive function definitions that utilize past happenings relationships. These definitions serve a purpose in verifying properties of real-time systems, as an event occurring at a specific point doesn't guarantee the same occurrence at another point in time, providing a key principle in real-time system design and analysis.

This study aimed to improve the prediction of instantaneous wall-pressure fluctuations in turbulent flows at a flat surface. We modified the model by Gualtieri et al., which relates wall-pressure correlations to large-scale coherent structures in the log-layer of wall-bounded flows, by using data from specific experiments and two other studies. These adjustments included calculating two particular constants based on pressure-strain terms and a correlation coefficient representing the strength of wall-pressure and streamwise velocity connections. While our model shows favorable performance in matching the fluctuation level of wall-pressure signals, further research is required to refine the prediction of timing and amplitude of pressure maxima.

We've introduced a new Born-Infeld model that incorporates Skyrme terms, focusing on its infant version for small values of $k/c$, utilizing a gauge-invariant formulation for effective analysis. By expanding the Higgs function in a sphere-truncated polynomial series, we derive an algebraic representation of the energy functional and its associated equations of motion. This results reveal the existence of self-dual Skyrme-Born-Infird models (BISky) infant solitons exhibiting scalability and spherical symmetry. Moreover, we demonstrate the possibility of mapping the BISky infant solitons to those of the infant Maxwell-Born-Infird models (MBI) using a conformal transformation. This relationship holds for both the one- and two-soliton configurations of MBI, which in turn are found to be self-dual as well.

In this study, we investigated the properties of Dirac and Weyl semimetals when subjected to a combined magnetic and periodic drive. The interaction between these two drives creates a complex pattern of gaps and loops in the energy spectrum, leading to the formation of semimetallic state with a singular momentum space topology. The emergence of this new phase is tied to the diabolical singularities present in the semimetal's momentum space. The appearance of time-reversal-violating Weyl semimetal states, on the other hand, relies on the number of momentum loops each Weyl mode occupies. The time-reversal-violating Weyl semimetal state exhibits several unique characteristics such as time-reversal-violating quantized Berry curvature, a topological invariant in three-dimensional systems, and the absence of a time-reversal symmetry protected topological phase. The time-reversal-violating Weyl semimetal state also displays a unique quantized magnetoelectric effect. The number of time-reversal-violating Weyl semimetal states and their locations within the phase diagram can be controlled by adjusting the strength of the periodic drive. The time-reversal-violating Weyl semimetal state can also be quantized by adjusting the intensity of the periodic drive when an integer number of momentum loops is occupied by each Weyl mode.

Developing novel, coherent light sources with the assistance of nanoantennas is beneficial for the creation of single-photon emitters, though they often suffer from low efficiency due to limited light coupling. To address this challenge, researchers have proposed a new approach that combines optical hybridization and enhanced radiation capabilities. This innovative method was successfully tested using a specific nanostructure composed of a quantum emitter and two Fano resonant metal-dielectric cavities. The observed results indicate an impressive enhancement of radiation efficiency by nearly two orders of magnitude. The mechanism of this enhancement involves the interaction of two distinct Fano resonances, one of which is generated by geometric effects and the other by electron oscillations. The principles underlying this technique can be applied to designing and optimizing coiled dielectric and plasmonic nanostructures for the amplification of light emission.

Researchers conducted an experiment and simulation to study electric double layer screening in a granular material. The material used consisted of monodisperse polystyrene spheres of varying sizes immersed in a electrolyte solution. The goal was to test a theoretical model that predicts unusual screening properties. An experimental technique was developed to measure the effective charge of the aggregate of smaller particles, which differed from the individual particles. The results revealed that the collective charge of the smaller particles was less negative than expected, leading to a prolonged screening length. These findings were supported by a computational model that simulated the interactions between the particles. The data also showed a strong correlation between the aggregate's electrical properties and its structural state, which was further confirmed by microscale observations of the particles' behavior.

Investigations of experimentally produced silicene on hexagonal boron nitride substrates reveal that decorating the edges with manganese impurities alters the material's magnetic properties. The resulting alignment of Mn impurities confers a spontaneous magnetization quenching effect, supplanting Mn's magnetization with that of the host material. The present research utilizes a multilayer model and incorporates GGA+U calculations to analyze the results. Two distinct phases of Mn-doped silicene are studied: an A honeycomb phase which develops a Dirac cone on the edge of the convex hexagon manganese and B honeycomb phases which form at the concave vertices of the hexagon. Our research indicates that A honeycomb phases demonstrate metallic characteristics along with spontaneous ferromagnetic ordering, whereas B honeycomb phases are seen to be half-metallic with a tendency towards a spin-dimer phase at half filling. The findings show that A and B honeycomb phases change from metallic to half-metallic states as they transition from the edge to the vertex of the hexagon. The research also reveals that decoating the manganese impurities results in the transformation of the A honeycomb phase into a B phase via a pair of edge dislocations. The results of this study support the theory that manganese impurities form lines or walls in manganese-doped silicene, running along the boundaries between the sublattices. The present research indicates that a metallic state forms at half filling in the manganese-doped sil

The formation of a young stellar object (YSS) is crucial to understanding the process of star formation in a 10,000 solar mass compact molecular core (CMC) like Sgr A East. An analysis of the core's properties indicates that the YSS must have a initial mass much greater than 20 times the mass of our sun. This is because only a massive initial core will produce a massive final star. The critical age for the core is 1-3 million years. The core's central density must be around 10,000 times higher than the local interstellar medium, and its temperature is likely similar to the interstellar medium. The core's total mass is approximately 10,000 solar masses and its dimensions are around 50 astronomical units in size. A massive outflow from the core's nose can explain the observed PDS-70 H$_2$ emission, which is equivalent to about 5$\times$10$^{-4}$ solar units in volume. The core's central pressure is around 3$\times$10$^{-11}$ bars, and its total density is around 10$^{-18}$ g cm$^{-3}$. The core's central pressure and density are similar to those of other efficiently accreting young stars, which is consistent with the predictions of self-regulating accretion theory. This paper investigates the efficacy of six synthetic oversampling methods in three-class and ten-class text classification. Unique to this research, the impacts of two forms of oversampling are explored – combining instances and consolidating classes – utilizing two classes with imbalanced data and a third serving as a control. The findings indicate that building class clusters yields superior performance across the board, with particular success in augmenting the evaluation of scarce classes while minimizing errors in the other categories. Conversely, the combination of instances results in enhanced classification of the dominant class while failing to improve performance for the other classes. The research further reveals that the benefits of oversampling techniques are more pronounced in scenarios with more significant class imbalances. The outcomes of this study hold significant implications for the practical application of these methods in real-world situations.

This study analyzes the connection between COVID-19 coverage in the US and the region's actual experiences, focusing on news outlets from diverse areas and their reporting habits. An online survey revealed significant disparities in COVID-related news coverage among regional outlets, with areas hit hard by the pandemic receiving more attention from a larger number of news sources. Areas severely affected by the virus were found to receive coverage from larger numbers of sources, but also saw fewer sources compared to less affected regions dominate the narrative. An investigation of 633 regions, 328 of which were designated as "high-risk" and 305 as "low-risk" by the CDC, showed that regions classified as high-risk received 25% more COVID-related coverage and were covered by 43% more sources. A deeper analysis of 1,893 individual news sources showed that regions classified as high-risk were dominated by sources that also covered other areas classified as high-risk. An analysis of 11 million articles indicated that a smaller percentage of sources, primarily those in high-risk regions, drove COVID-related coverage in both high-risk and low-risk areas. Furthermore, an analysis of 20 million audience records revealed that audiences in high-risk regions were comprised of individuals who also consumed news from sources that covered COVID-related topics more frequently in high-risk regions. The findings suggest that audiences in high-risk regions are exposed to COVID-related coverage by a smaller number of diverse news sources.

The Rapid Multipole Algorithm, a recent variant of the Desloge-Moulton method, has efficient implementations for solving N-body problems but raises concerns about maintaining total angular momentum due to potential issues with the way it handles multipoles and translation terms. Research, including our own, had assumed the Rapid Multipole Algorithm preserved total angular momentum, which led us to develop an incorrect proof. However, this proof was later disproven by counterexamples showing the method does not always conserve total angular momentum. We also present additional flaws in a previously claimed non-optimizing implementation of the algorithm and provide a counterexample showing it failed to conserve total angular momentum in the Hénon algorithm, which is a non-optimizing version of the Desloge-Moulton method.

Research into the detailed characteristics of the initial and final states of polarization in virtual and real Compton scattering has a long history. Although real Compton scattering on a polarized target automatically possesses initial and final polarization, an explicit examination of the transition from the initial to the final polarization is needed for the specific case of elastic electron-proton scattering. This article investigates the specific case of electron-proton scattering where the electron and proton are initially polarized along the same direction. A precise calculation is performed using the Gennes-Bartenmann framework, taking into account the full gluon-dependent non-zero virtual photon polarization vector. The calculation reveals that, despite the asymmetry effect of gluon exchange, polarization $ P_F $ of the final proton remains the same as $ P_I $, the initial polarization of the proton, and is independent of the four-momentum transfer $ t $. This result agrees with previous, less detailed calculations and confirms expectations based on physical considerations. An additional calculation, using a different framework, was also carried out for comparison with these previous results.

In a scenario where a model needs to be trained or improved, it might not have access to complete data sets. This could be due to the cost of collecting or processing the data. In such cases, the model can try to transfer knowledge from a related model that has had access to the full data sets. This process is known as knowledge transfer or communication. The model that transfers knowledge is the teacher and the model being trained is the student. The teacher needs to convey the important information to the student, but this can be a complex task, especially when dealing large datasets. In this study, we are looking at ways to improve knowledge transfer by finding shortcuts, so the student can learn more efficiently. We evaluated several methods and found that under certain conditions, some techniques perform better than others. The conditions that influence performance involve the balance between different data samples, the similarity between data samples, and the consistency of the teacher's messages.

A thorough examination of proton-proton collisions is conducted to identify Higgs boson pairs (HH) produced in conjunction with a vector boson (W or Z). The analysis relies on a dataset amounting to 139 inverse femtobarns of data recorded by the ATLAS detector at the Large Hadron Collider during the 2015-2018 period. To categorize HHZ and HHW events, different kinematic ranges are used for the vector boson. To determine the various backgrounds in each case, data are compared to simulated predictions and control regions. No significant excess above predicted backgrounds is found in any of the categories. As a result, the 95% confidence level observed limit is set at 7.7 fb for HHZ and 10 fb for HHW HH production in the [125 + 125] geq [110, 230] GeV mass range. These results surpass expected expectations by 2.0, 2.3, 2.2, 2.0 and 1.8 standard deviations for the different vector boson categories. Furthermore, the predicted sensitivity is achieved for the vector boson categories except for the lowest mass region of HHZ, where expected sensitivity is 0.7 standard deviations lower.

Achieving population inversion in an electric field, without relying on optical pumping, is a feasible option for constructing novel laser materials. Theoretical models and experimental demonstrations have shown that certain atoms can be prepared in a highly excited state through electronic transition and then efficiently lase. However, this process is limited to specific conditions and may not be applicable to all atom species. Notably, using a laser medium that does not rely on optical pumping presents a significant advantage in terms of simplicity and potential applications. Here, a proposed laser concept is based on an electronically pumped cesium medium, which is capable of supporting a long gain medium to produce narrow linewidth laser emissions. To further develop this idea, a prototype was constructed using a miniature laser cavity and a heated cesium vapor source within a Stark cell, which is capable of producing stable single-mode laser emissions at specific frequencies when an appropriate electric field is applied. The system's performance can be optimized by adjusting the Stark shift and achieving a population inversion that favors the lower laser level, thus enabling two-photon emissions of 1313 nm lasers at a stable output.

Let's consider a K3 variety defined by the period matrix $\Omega$, its associated Neron lattice, and its amphitoriginal covering relationship with a rational Jacobian variety. We introduce the concept of a period lattice being almost generated by $\Omega$. This almost generation criterion provides an updated version of Zilber-Pink's theorems applying to K3 varieties, leveraging the use of functorial methods, and analyzes their applications within toric geometry contexts. We observe that almost generating the period lattice offers an alternative way to the Shafarevich conjecture's validity in certain toric scenarios, and these findings extend previous results on Siegel disks, which were previously proven via Siegel's theorem, and can be applied to achieve analogous outcomes with the $\overline{\partial}$-equation's fundamental solutions.

In the context of the super-symmetric extension of the Standard Model, specifically within the framework of the minimal supersymmetric standard model, it's acknowledged that the mass of the neutral Higgsino is substantial. Considering this, a novel decomposing neutralino has been introduced with a configuration of (x1,y1,x2,y2). Assuming an extended role for the right-handed neutrino as a mediator in dark matter interactions and a mass of approximately 6.3 MeV for it, the resulting neutralino's gamma spectrum has been calculated under the MoND theory, characterized by a non-uniform interaction between particles. The interaction in the model is model-dependent and non-relativistic. The possibility of the neutralino as a potential dark matter candidate has also been explored, with a discussion on its relevance to recent observations.

A new polynomial-time method has been developed that can approximate the genus of a dense graph, where the genus represents the fewest number of planes required to embed the graph without edges intersecting. Given a large number of samples, this method can estimate the genus of any dense graph with a high level of accuracy. For a specific graph, the estimated genus can be as accurate as the actual genus, or vice versa, within some limit of accuracy. This approach leverages a specific type of embedding called an abstract embedding and relies on an effective volume metric. It works by first establishing accurate estimates for a specific reference graph, referred to as the Kornoukhov graph, and then employs these estimates as a basis for the genus estimation method.

This paper presents a decentralized algorithm, dubbed RN-DCO, to solve large-scale distributed convex optimization problems. RN-DCO is based on an randomized Newton method and shows superiority over existing decentralized algorithms, such as DEC-SN, by achieving a 2-2$\gamma$-scaled optimal solution after $N$ iterations, where $N$ represents the number of nodes and $\gamma$ accounts for communication delay loss due to communication constraints. Furthermore, RN-DCO is computationally efficient as it only utilizes first-order oracle access and encloses the convergence rate of current best-in-class methods, such as HPDecomposition, while outperforming other decentralized algorithms, including JSACCO, DEC-SN, and DECAMP. The efficacy of RN-DCO is validated through experiments in machine learning applications.

This study focuses on developing and evaluating hate-speech detection techniques for Hindi and Bengali, utilizing neural networks. The research team, Arx Anomaly, participating in the Hate-speech Challenge 2022, submitted entries for both the identification and classification tasks. The analysis presents a novel language model based on bidirectional GRUs for each language, employing pre-trained word embeddings from a common source. The model was trained on combined datasets of positive and negative samples for each language, defying conventional practices. The research also explores the effect of varying training sizes on performance and offers a transfer learning application. The team achieved second place in the classification task and initially ranked fourth in the identification task, later surpassed by newer submissions. The analysis details challenges encountered and strategies adopted to navigate the competition.

In particle detection by Gas Time Projection Chambers, the straight line path of ionizing particles is disrupted by recoil momentum acquired from nucleus-scattering events. This detection challenge presents an opportunity to utilize recoil detection to bypass the limitations of nucleus rejection, thereby making it possible to employ sensitive detectors, despite the presence of abundant radioactive contamination. To leverage recoil detection, it's essential to develop observables that can identify recoiling parent-nuclei, while minimizing a significant issue: false positives triggered by the detector's own radiative contaminants. To address this, a novel observable called the Recoil Poleplane is introduced, along with two comparison alternatives: the Focal Recoil and the Energy-Momentum Vector products of the collision and Recoil Particle candidate. Simulation-based testing using a representative event with Recoil has been conducted to assess the effectiveness of these observables in both Recoil and Non-Recoil scenarios, while investigating the impact of various event kinematics and detector resolution. The Recoil Poleplane has demonstrated superior performance and robustness across a wide range of conditions, and it's expected that this recoil detection approach will play a significant role in future high-precision searches for hidden particles at angles of a few milliradians relative to the parent particle trajectory.

A crucial capability for commercial driving is making smart choices in high-pressure situations, which involves deciding the best action to take given specific context and time constraints. For a major ride-hailing company, we created a set of choices for drivers to follow, which includes leaving early for pickups, arriving late to drop-offs, or speeding up en-route. To help drivers make the best decisions, the system known as Challenger generates alternative choices for them to follow, which are based on the company's rules and guidelines. Our new Challenger II system not only considers these rules, but also takes into account the context of the situation, such as traffic and time of day, to make more informed decisions. By testing the system, we found that it leads to better customer reviews, more tips, and higher ratings for the drivers. Moreover, we discovered that certain behaviors of the drivers that were previously seen as negative, such as leaving early for pickups, can actually become positive behaviors given the context of the situation.

At the NeurIPS 2020 workshop, the out-of-context learning challenge presented a new concept where model evaluations based on downstream performance were just as important as traditional measures. This report outlines key points from the workshop discussion and serves as a summary of the challenge, featuring a repeat of the challenge, a high-level model comparison, and additional reflection on the event.

A Gaussian stochastic field creates a connection between a parameter space and a space of functions, allowing us to explore the parameter space based on the field's geometry. Hisakazu Komiya developed the concept of geodesic paths in the Gaussian stochastic field's parameter space, finding them useful in control engineering. Conversely, this research investigates geodesic paths in the field itself, using the method of stochastic differential equations to analyze these paths through the means of Gaussian measures. Furthermore, computational tools are employed to illustrate the efficacy of the proposed method in the context of control engineering.

The experimental observation of surface height anisotropy through dynamical length measurements involving leaping molecules impacting a structured anisotropic film surface is described. Molecules undergo periodic and vertically increasing oscillations over the film. Data on the period and velocity of these oscillations, which decrease with increasing kinetic energy of the molecules, are plotted and match theoretical predictions within experimental error. These findings provide direct experimental confirmation of the theoretical model of molecule-film interaction.

Using a multi-step approach and modular forms, we develop an understanding of how many unique values an L-function mod $l$ can take as a complex number, and establish the maximum possible bound on the magnitude of these values, depending on specific values of $l$ and the level of the associated modular form. This outcome specifically addresses a problem posed by Y. F. Sivak and M. Telybor, while also considering other related factors. Along the way, we establish a preliminary result regarding the movement of critical points in L-functions mod $l$. This outcome holds additional significance in its broader implications for the L-functions of maass forms, drawing connections to the Riemann Hypothesis along the way. Specifically, we demonstrate that the L-functions of maass forms satisfy certain conditions that lead to this hypothesis. This new insight is seen to be particularly significant when applied to a specific type of maass form with a weight of 10, associated with the coefficient 1. This form does not meet the requirements for being holomorphic or weakly holomorphic, nor does it meet the requirements for having vanishing weight. Nonetheless, we leverage its properties to the fullest extent possible. This approach allows us to analyze the behavior of the associated L-function and utilize that understanding to establish a new bound on the magnitude of zeros and critical points. This outcome holds implications for the distribution of zeros in the critical plane and satisfies the Riemann Hypothesis. This new insight is seen to

Research into spin-based technology holds significant potential for advancing data storage and processing efficiency. Graphene, a versatile graphene sheet, exhibits unique transport properties but lacks the necessary conditions for stable spin configurations. However, creating nanostructures from graphene's armchair orientation fulfills these requirements, allowing for spin-related properties to emerge. Our study explores the transport properties of such nanostructures under applied electric fields, focusing on defects and edge effects to control spin-like behavior. Calculations reveal spin-like behavior controllable through a gate bias, observable in spin-related properties including tunneling conductance and current, even in absence of actual spin. These findings provide valuable insights into manipulating spin-like transport in graphene-based technology.

The Korovkin theorem type results for weakly nonlinear and monotonic operators are developed, specifically for a class of multivariate polynomial operators that involve high-order derivatives and are applied in approximation theory using linear difference methods.

The concept of pancyclicity suggests that a graph $G$ contains an all-cycle subgraph. Researchers have made significant progress in understanding pancyclicity in specific types of graphs. For autonomous graphs, the definitions of Hamiltonicity, autonomy number, and pancyclicity align, making it a particularly intriguing topic. In this paper, we explore autonomous graphs and establish new criteria and bounds for autonomy numbers and pancyclicity in these graphs.

Our study calculates the directed flow of charged mesons and baryons from simulated heavy collisions. For the first time, we've investigated directed flow in collisions involving specific isotopes with varying strange matter content. Our findings reveal that the calculated directed flow coefficient $v_1$ follows a pattern influenced by centrality, beam momentum, and particle mass. A specific class of collisions involving isotopes with strange matter content appears to intensify the flow. These results can help further the development of a reliable transport theory that describes the initial stages of heavy collisions.

The spectral Koopman method has emerged as an effective technique for dynamic system analysis, particularly in applications requiring high precision. This approach uses Koopman operator theory to create a linear representation of nonlinear systems, enabling the use of linear spectral analysis techniques. Recent improvements to the spectral Koopman method have increased its versatility, allowing it to solve initial value problems and differentiate between stable and unstable dynamics more efficiently. Despite these advancements, applying the spectral Koopman method to complex systems can be computationally demanding, as it typically requires evaluating a large set of basis functions across the entire problem domain. This article presents a novel adaptation of the spectral Koopman method, which incorporates sparse grid methods to reduce the computational cost of complex systems analysis. The proposed approach can significantly decrease the computational cost of Koopman analysis by utilizing advanced sparse grid techniques, such as Clenshaw-Curtis quadrature-based methods. To evaluate the efficiency of this new formulation, the study compares the results of numerical simulations using the standard adaptive spectral Koopman method and the proposed sparse-grid-driven adaptive spectral Koopman method, demonstrating a substantial reduction in computational cost while maintaining high levels of accuracy.

This article outlines a novel approach called the outward complex scaling technique. It adapts the existing complex scaling method to investigate bound quantum systems under a strong external electric field. The outward complex scaling technique moves the imaginary part of the Hamiltonian operator outside the region of the finite system, where it remains invariant to translations. This approach allows us to efficiently investigate the behavior of atoms and molecules when they undergo a strong DC electric field, where it is linked with the Coulombic potential. A numerical program based on the outward complex scaling technique has been created and used to study the energy eigenvalues of the hydrogen atom molecule (HeH$^+$) and the water molecule (H$_2$O), both at their ground states, under the influence of a strong DC electric field.

The Sinkhorn algorithm is widely used for solving the Schrödinger problem which involves finding the optimal transport between two probability distributions. While this algorithm converges under certain conditions, there are scenarios where convergence is not guaranteed. This paper presents a counterexample demonstrating that the Sinkhorn algorithm may diverge when certain specific conditions are breached. Specifically, it shows that when the cost function is uniformly bounded from below and the source distribution is concentrated on a single point, the algorithm will indefinitely oscillate and move away from equilibrium. This example highlights the importance of source support restriction in ensuring the algorithm's performance. Furthermore, it is found that even with unbounded cost functions, the algorithm can still converge under certain specific distribution coupling conditions which are defined within this study.

The ATLAS experiment at the LHC recorded data from lead-lead collisions in 2018, which included top-quark pair creation events with the lead at a 5.02 TeV collision energy. This research focused on examining the top-quark pair creation cross-section ($\sigma_{\text{t}\overline{\text{t}}}$) in proton-proton collisions under the specified conditions. Utilizing proton-proton data from 2018, which covered a 25 pb$^{-1}$ dataset and was analyzed utilizing two selected categories, these results were subsequently scaled to match the lead-lead conditions. Specifically, fast atmospheric muon measurements in the Fast Interaction Trigger facilitated the adjustment for the number of participating nucleon pairs ($N_{\text{ch}}$) via rapidity density of charged particles. $\sigma_{\text{t}\overline{\text{t}}}$ in proton-proton collisions was then used to derive the corresponding value in lead-lead collisions. This research resulted in a lead-lead cross-section of approximately 2.03 $\pm$ 0.06 (statistical) $\pm$ 0.18 (syst.) $\mathrm{mb}$. The results were notably in line with the theoretical predictions from perturbative QCD, which stood at 1.26 $\mathrm{mb}$ for the relevant conditions.

This study examines the localized behavior of a technique called centrally linked localized particle system, which is developed from the traditional SLTS on a complex graph. The core connection represents a significant transformation between the two systems. The central bond triggers a phase shift in the localized particle's dynamics. It is shown that the eigenvalues of the stochastic matrix are real-valued or positively valued, resulting in two distinct type of localization behaviors - a symmetric or asymmetric type of localization, depending on the system's structure and its fundamental properties.

The geometric characteristics of Janezwo type functions are understood under certain conditions to be linked to generalized Bessel functions, and to investigate this connection completely, we establish connections between these functions and their relationship with generalized Bessel functions, ultimately leading to a definition that incorporates all possible cases.

Income inequality is a pressing concern that affects many cities worldwide. To explore its potential impact on spatial dynamics, we investigated the behavior of urban residents in multiple cities using mobile device data. We analyzed users' activities and found that during the COVID-19 pandemic, individuals from lower income areas exhibited a more significant shift towards staying home and avoided public spaces compared to their higher income counterparts. Consequently, this behavior contributed to a broader dispersal of urban residents and increased inequalities in public space usage among different income groups.

Our research focuses on the study of preconditioning techniques for two-phase flow simulations within irregular porous media. We examine and compare the effectiveness of various nonlinear field-split preconditioning methods in handling steady-state two-phase flow problems with disparities in their physical properties. We evaluate and improve three techniques - Simple Color Field Presumption, Random Field Presumption, and Randomized Presumption - and establish that the Randomized Presumption is the most efficient, especially when coupled with Newton's method, outperforming the other methods regardless of the initial arrangement of the fields. This is largely due to its ability to adapt to all field configurations, achieving local consistency and minimizing the number of necessary iterations. We also conclude that the simplicity of the Simple Color Field Presumption is desirable but that the Randomized Presumption is the most suitable choice overall.

A innovative optical cavity design is proposed, created using pairs of chiral nanoparticles that reflect light in a specific asymmetrical pattern. When an plane wave is directed at these pairs, the average optical field exhibits a chirality properties in one direction. Furthermore, the design can be modified to allow for tunable optical chirality by adjusting the cavity's dimensions. Additionally, the research demonstrates that even at high frequencies, the cavity's properties can be maintained due to a gap in resonance frequencies between the pairs of nanoparticles. This leads to a phenomenon where nearby particles remain in sync while particles at longer distances are out of sync. This property may contribute to the development of novel optical devices, including those that control and manipulate light with high degrees of polarization.

We key in on a specific boundary condition in Liouville CFT, specifically tailored for the Seiberg bound, and thoroughly investigate this model. Our work is supported by various tools, notably the use of meromorphic Lagrangian path integral techniques, verifications of Cardy's consistency conditions, and most significantly, the derivation of two-point and three-point function expressions through a first-order action approach. These outcomes are then compared with the existing results for Seiberg bound in Liouville CFT, and we predict that this developed boundary condition can be linked to a specific classical matrix model solution related to JT gravity.

This article explores various solutions for an ideal fluid-based warp drive model incorporating the cosmological constant and gravitational potential. By classifying these solutions into three categories, we examine their potential cosmological implications. However, due to the presence of complex singularities in the models, their practical application in space propulsion remains uncertain.

As cities' physical and digital infrastructures increasingly depend on intelligent systems, a disconnection between the two is felt more and not less, causing inefficiencies to rise. Isolation of digital models from city planning further hinders optimal city design, but merging these elements can boost a city's quality of life and its economic potential if done with a unified vision.

This research proposes the creation of a common platform to manage and govern city data to address this disparity, promoting standardized data collection and analysis while allowing for adaptable and location-specific strategies.

A multi-faceted approach is taken to this problem with three primary objectives. Firstly, developing a common platform for data management will facilitate the creation of a uniform understanding of urban data. Secondly, establishing a shared protocol for data collection will enable cities to compare and learn from one another. Thirdly, embracing such frameworks will allow cities to control who accesses and uses their data.

Guides, the CITYLAB@MIT project's initial prototype, has been tested with successful outcomes, and its findings provide a foundation for future data-driven initiatives.

Using the Mott-ISMR experiment's unique properties, such as hundreds of thousands of collective spin states and highly sensitive readout methods, we investigate the effects of spin dephasing in two-dimensional ion crystals. We observe a specific type of dephasing known as Bragg dephasing and provide an accurate mathematical representation of it based on the lattice's structure and the movement of the ions. Our research examines how ion movement is influenced by various factors, such as thermal energy, intermolecular potentials, and laser cooling. The study of Bragg dephasing provides a highly sensitive means to measure the average kinetic energy of the ions, enabling us to detect minor increases in temperature following the completion of laser cooling. Additionally, we discuss how this technique could be employed to investigate the momentum distributions of the ions.

A new quantum-mechanical approach has been developed, taking into account the interactions between a terahertz probe and a hydrogen fluoride dimer molecular junction. The method accurately models the effects of electromagnetic fields and the redistribution of electrons within the probe's electric field. Results obtained demonstrate a significant increase in the charge density at the tip of the probe, especially for lower energy terahertz fields. These findings support the hypothesis that the high sensitivity of certain TERS experiments is attributable to a localized hot spot formed by electron charging. It has also been shown that certain TERS experiments may be influenced by charge transfer or rehybridization effects, leading to an alternative explanation of non-terahertz frequency vibrations in CO groups. Furthermore, the new method has the potential to enable the assignment of spectral components to specific atomic or group vibrations within the probe molecule.

We conducted K-band observations of 19 galaxies near our Milky Way using the Sardinia Radio Telescope's real-time capabilities to search for synthetic microwave background radiation, focusing on frequencies between 28 and 32 GHz. These observations were carried out between July 2019 and January 2020. So far, we have detected an intense signal from the Milky Way and three galaxies, particularly NGC 253, NGC 55, and IC 0110, which can be attributed to Cosmic Microwave Background radiation over an extended period of time.

Researchers have been trying to understand how materials change properties in response to external stimuli for centuries, and have developed multiple theoretical frameworks to explain these changes. However, there is still a significant gap in knowledge about the relationship between changes in entropy and the material's internal structure. A new study has shed light on this gap by investigating the changes in entropy in a particular type of crystal when it ferroelectrics or caloric. The study used advanced simulations to reveal that a particular type of vibration within the crystal lattice is responsible for the observed entropy changes, and these vibrations weaken the material's internal structure. The results of this study correlate well with experimental data and provide new insights into the connection between crystal structure, vibration, and the material's internal stability.

A proposed model for a quantum system, based on the 228-dimensional complexification of the $E_8$ lattice, is investigated here, including its potential for physical implementation. We explore the full Clifford group generated by complexifications of the root and weight lattice generators of $E_8$. Our study focuses on a specific subgroup generated by 40 simple unitary operators that can be effectively implemented in current quantum hardware, considering the spinor group and its relationship with weight lattice complexifications. We demonstrate that approximately 86% of all Clifford covariant pure states exhibit a visible quantum effect, defined as a measurable difference in overlap with non-covariant counterparts, using a specific measure. Moreover, about 44% of all covariant pure states exhibit a significant quantum effect, defined as a substantial difference in overlap with non-covariant counterparts, using the same measure. Our research also shows that approximately 85% of all covariant pure states exhibit a clear contextu-ality effect, defined as a substantial difference in overlap with non-covariant counterparts, using the same measure. These results indicate that the proposed model is an excellent system for investigating quantum information, due to its potential for extensive research on quantum entanglement and contextuality. Furthermore, the model's 880-dimensional space of pure qudents matches previous findings on the 878-dimensional space of qudents in the $E8$ lattice system, establishing an isomorphism between the two systems.

For any two series with discrete values, a bounding radius in the Euclidean space can be found within a specific interval, which allows for the approximation of a single point within that radius, resembling the nearest neighbor problem. Similarly, a problem involving k-nearest neighbors can be solved by identifying n k-nearest neighbors, each spaced at least a certain distance apart, both problems being solvable in logarithmic time with the use of k-d trees. However, it has been demonstrated that such methods can only approximate the ideal radius and neighbor positions. Furthermore, it has been shown that for any given set of possible radius values, it is possible to find a radius and a point within that set, thus showing the previously known bounds are the best possible. A related problem, the closest neighbor problem, has also been explored and it has been demonstrated that it is not possible to find a single radius that applies to all possible closest neighbor positions.

High-precision quantum experiments face a major limitation in measurement error due to the uncertainty principle. Recent research has produced various error-reduction techniques, notably single-shot error rejection via post-processing and more effective approaches leveraging pre-processing and intermediate error correction. However, these methods can only partially alleviate measurement errors. In this context, we present a new technique called iterative Bayesian error reduction that integrates other error-reduction methods and significantly reduces the total error in the measurement process. We demonstrate that IBER achieves a substantial error decrease in the range from single-shot to multi-shot scenarios, and these results can be further enhanced by integrating it with other error-reduction methods that focus on multi-shot error reduction. In particular, we show that a three-step process combining single-shot error correction via post-processing, IBER, and single-shot error rejection yields an error reduction exceeding $10^6$, a gain of over two orders of magnitude more than previously known techniques.

A well-established standard allows a device to seamlessly integrate with a variety of compatible systems.  Historically, standards in human-robot interaction focus on physical interaction rather than informational, and the presence of multiple incompatible standards often hinders adoption across the board. For people with intellectual disabilities, using a mobile map can be a helpful feature in navigating unfamiliar areas, but creating and maintaining maps is challenging due to the need for constant updating when environments change. To address this issue, we suggest an easy-to-use mapping system based on a hierarchical topological layout representation, which simplifies the creation and modification of maps and integrates well with existing accessibility apps. The concept of topological maps, which focuses on place connections rather than exact locations, is particularly beneficial for users who rely on simple interface designs. To facilitate user interaction with the map, we developed a visual interface using icon sets and designed corresponding input methods, including voice commands and gestures. The addition of spatial audio feedback and offline-accessible destination input enables users to discover and select places on the map. The system allows users to mark locations of interest using landmarks' descriptions, which can then be accessed through voice commands or gestures. The system incorporates text-to-speech and speech recognition functionality, enabling users to input places' descriptions when discovering new locations.

This paper introduces a novel method for developing two classes of inter-group complementary code sets. The proposed binary Z-Complementary Array Code Sets are defined using multivariable functions over finite fields. The auto- and cross-correlation properties of these code sets are extensively examined. Computer simulations confirm the satisfactory performance of the suggested codes.

We present an optimization-based framework for CT image reconstruction that can automatically select the number of materials, handle incomplete data, and characterize each material's physical properties. Given that CT scanners produce multiple energy beams with data subject to noise, we apply a penalized-likelihood model that incorporates a prior to steer image reconstruction. Our method utilizes a differentiable model to characterize materials, reduces noise through a principal component analysis-based prior, and selects the number of materials through an analysis of eigenvalues. Results show that our method outperforms state-of-the-art techniques, including DeepImageReconstructor, for a range of phantom and physical material data.

We investigate the influence of electron spillover and nonlocality on the physics of gap plasmons in the limit where the gap size approaches zero. Using a numerical solution, we combine a one-dimensional model with a finite-element method and consider two types of arrangements: a gapless structure with a single plate and a larger particle spanning multiple gaps. Furthermore, we introduce an adiabatic approximation to study the transition between these limiting cases. Our findings demonstrate that by taking electron spillover into account, the predicted plasmon frequency in the single-plate scenario matches the result for superconducting graphene when the gap size is zero. Notably, if we consider a larger particle spanning several gaps without a gap, the predicted plasmon frequency can be influenced significantly by nonlocality, whereas when the same particle is divided by an ultra-thin gap, nonlocal contributions become relatively smaller in comparison to other influences.

The evaluation of contextual information about named entities is essential in extracting significant terms from text. However, determining what is significant can vary across entities, as well as depend on the specific task and information required for each one. In this research, we address the issue of extracting contextual names from academic papers by using the nameless entities present in the abstracts and citations as a benchmark. Our approach involves training a model to identify terms with significant properties - being a name, having previous occurrences, and being related to the entity - through multi-task learning, where each entity is analyzed in conjunction with other namehood-related tasks. Our results demonstrate that employing context knowledge to address these tasks leads to a substantial boost in our overall performance. Our experiments also show that employing contextual information has a much greater impact than relying solely on signal from the individual words. Additionally, we found that our method outperforms alternative baselines that use contextual information for extracting contextual names.

Displaying detailed information, such as medical records or genetic sequences, poses a challenge in visual analysis due to its compact display and interactivity requirements. This paper provides a comprehensive review of recent research on visual analysis interactions and proposes a set of design guidelines for effectively rendering large datasets on small screens. Specifically, the paper explores the trade-offs involved in representing individual data points, discussing the pros and cons of sequential, summary, and hybrid views. It also examines visualization techniques for highlighting interesting regions within large datasets and facilitates zooming, browsing, and drilling down into the data. Furthermore, the paper discusses advancements in longitudinal information visualization and outlines research directions for creating interactive visualizations that showcase temporal or sequential data. This research has far-reaching implications, and the corresponding paper has been published at CHI 2021.

In recent years, there has been significant interest in developing AI models that integrate diverse medical record data. This encompasses various data types such as clinical notes, imaging, genomic data, environmental factors, and social media information. However, current approaches primarily focus on structured clinical data, leaving a significant research gap regarding a comprehensive aggregation of unstructured and structured clinical information. This issue is particularly prominent in real-world settings where clinical decisions heavily rely on unstructured observation notes. This paper proposes a novel method to address this challenge by developing a graph neural network model capable of analyzing both structured and unstructured clinical information. Specifically, the proposed model uses a unique transformer-based framework to analyze diverse medical record data. This involves capturing clinical note attributes through a transformer encoder, which generates comprehensive observation embeddings that a graph neural network model utilizes to make predictions. The proposed model has been evaluated on a large electronic health record dataset and has demonstrated superior performance in predicting patient outcomes. Notably, the proposed model has achieved a 2% increased AUROC value compared to existing models, which highlights its effectiveness in clinical prediction tasks.

Within the context of electric double layer on a flexible membrane, we examine the relationship between system energy and the membrane's conformation in response to varying external voltages and concentrations of ions. Considering the dynamic nature of the solvent, we develop a model based on a modified Poisson-Boltzmann equation and perform rigorous self-consistent field calculations. Our results show that accounting for solvent polarization significantly affects the distribution of ions near the membrane, particularly at high concentrations, thereby influencing the electrostatic potential and flexibility of the membrane. Additionally, we investigate the interplay between flexibility and electrical properties, finding that increased flexibility intensify the electrostatic properties of the membrane.

Although many software systems have been developed over the years, their development history, also known as software heritage, has often been lost. Reverse engineering an older software system to understand its operation and maintain it can be very challenging if no documentation or original developers are available. In cases where knowledge was recorded in unstructured text format, such as old project specifications or email conversations, extracting and utilizing this information to regain the software's knowledge heritage proves difficult. A recent study applied information retrieval techniques to convert unstructured text into specified functional requirements for a software system. The proposed approach successfully preserved the original data's semantics and was evaluated using datasets from two diverse software systems, demonstrating its general applicability to various systems, regardless of their complexity or domain. The methodology, called the text2requirement tool, outperformed comparable methods in multiple benchmarking tests and achieved promising results, indicating its potential to aid software maintenance and reconstruction efforts.

This research investigates a multi-objective energy-efficient strategy for wireless networks that incorporate relay deployment through network coding, particularly in wireless networks exhibiting diverse arrival rates and unevenly distributed power levels. To address this challenge, a comprehensive framework is established to minimize total network power consumption, encompassing both direct and relay-based transmission, while simultaneously ensuring a specified minimum data transfer rate for each source node. To achieve optimized outcomes, a collaborative algorithm is developed that integrates multiple techniques, including a set of predictive models, an iterative allocation model, and a power allocation model grounded in maximum cumulative rate, along with a multi-objective optimization model. The resulting model enables the allocation of relays and distribution of power across nodes in a manner that minimizes overall network power while ensuring high-quality data transfer. To verify its efficacy, the proposed strategy is tested in a multi-class network scenario and compared with a baseline method utilizing traditional fixed power levels, revealing a substantial power savings potential, averaging 30% to 40%. Furthermore, a multidimensional optimization approach allows for the identification of energy-efficient solutions even in large and complex networks, while demonstrating sensitivity to varying relay capabilities.

In order to investigate the YSR states produced by a magnetic impurity on a superconducting Nb(110) surface, an initial principles time-dependent nonequilibrium Green functions method is employed to create a relativistic impurity model. This model is based on an expanded Yu--Shiraishi--Rusinov (YSR) impurity model, incorporating particle-hole symmetry, and considers superconductivity, magnetic coupling, and relativistic effects. It accurately incorporates the minority spin impurity states that are influenced by exchange interactions and spin-orbit effects. This model is applied to an Mn adatom and magnetic dimers on the Nb(110) surface with a BCS critical temperature of 10.5 K. Our findings show that an Mn adatom sits in a hole state within the Nb gap due to strong magnetic effects. However, an Mn impurity situated adjacent to a vacancy on the Nb surface intermixes with Nb states both within and beyond the gap. This behavior differs from an Mn dimmer situated perpendicular to the Nb surface which intermixes primarily with Nb states at the Fermi level. Moreover, an Mn impurity situated parallel to the Nb surface exhibits YSR states positioned within the Nb gap. However, an Mn dimmer situated parallel to the Nb surface solely exhibits a large responisiveness to a nonequilibrium photon at low energy, positioned outside of the Nb gap.
