An experimental investigation of the K+ to pi+ v vbar process has been conducted using a K+ decays-in-flight dataset collected at the J-PARC Hadron Experimental Facility. The sample consisted of 6.1 x 10^8 K+ decays that were generated from a 23 GeV/c proton beam and a material target, resulting in a concentraton of pipe volumes containing K+. Following the pipe volumes, the K+ decays were embedded within a magnetic environment and were detected by a comprehensive detector system consisting of two large dipole magnets and 44 layers of different sensitive material. Within the detector's acceptance region, the 1 sigma (3 sigma) limit of the branching ratio for K+ to pi+ v vbar is estimated to be 0.55 x 10^-10 (2.6 x 10^-10), and it is anticipated that further enhancements to the experiment will result in a limit of 0.89 x 10^-10 (1.68 x 10^-10) by 2021.

Existing research has thoroughly investigated the challenges of reducing delays and biases in simultaneous localization and mapping. This study instead focuses on the challenges associated with using localization methods based on precomputed maps for robots distributing services in unfamiliar environments. We recognize that current approaches, which use statistical decision theory to balance delay and accuracy, are not effective in reducing prejudice in service delivery. This is because these methods tend to prioritize map quality over actual localization accuracy. To address this issue, we propose a new method that employs deep neural networks to analyze the context in which localization accuracy is evaluated and adjusts the delay-prejudice tradeoff accordingly. Further information about the dataset used in this study can be found at https://github.com/linlin Huang/DNN_filter_dataset.

Satellite images hold significant value for multiple applications due to their high spatial resolution and detailed texture characteristics. Understanding edge structures within these images is essential for identifying geographical features, transforming data into usable information, and addressing complex vision tasks. In image analysis, edges serve as crucial landmarks that separate distinct areas, and their identification paves the way for various subsequent processing steps, including classification, compression, and super-resolution. While deep learning techniques have achieved significant success in automated edge detection, they are often marred by performance instability and a lack of interpretability. In response, we have developed an innovative, formally grounded approach that relies on the Habib's edge detector, whose simplicity and reliability make it an attractive alternative. This approach leverages differential operators to create accurate edge maps, and can be easily integrated into real-time applications without requiring extensive training. The proposed solution is robust and efficient, and produces consistent results, outperforming other methods on multiple benchmark datasets. Its compact size and fast processing speed allow it to effectively operate on embedded systems, and we have successfully demonstrated this capability on a Raspberry Pi device.

A rate equation model is developed and solved analytically for the evolution of a two-level system with multiple competing resonances. The model's solution yields an analytical formula for the time-dependent absorption coefficient, which shows that the system behaves as a non-interacting system in the long time limit. The model's framework enables the inclusion of an arbitrary number of resonances and predicts that the system's behavior will be influenced by internal competition among resonances. The validity of the model is demonstrated through a comparison with complex Monte Carlo simulations. The model's equations are formulated in a manner analogous to a hydrogen atom energy dispersion relationship, providing insight into the conditions under which the model's approximations hold.

To ensure the reliability of modulation recognition systems, it's critical to safeguard them against malicious attacks. The vulnerability of machine learning-based methods to adversarial threats has been a area of research within signal processing community. Given that the performance of Deep Neural Networks can be impaired by tiny alterations in input data, it's a pressing concern. A new approach presented in this letter uses blended Generative Adversarial Networks to generate adversarial examples that can help signal processing community understand the degree of vulnerability. A test was conducted using BL-GAN on signals from both BPSK and QPSK formats with 1000 samples in each set, yielding results that show the efficacy of blended GANs in creating adversarial examples, highlighting QPSK's increased vulnerability.

Segmentation of Multiple Sclerosis lesions is a challenging task that medical imaging community has struggled with for over two decades. Recent models based on deep learning have shown considerable progress in achieving disease burden assessment and predictive analytics for patient outcomes. Nonetheless, deep learning models trained on data from one institution or clinical group are often not transferable to other settings, leading to a research gap on sequential adaptation or continuous learning methods for segmentation tasks. This study addresses this issue by developing a new approach to segment lesions that adapts to new datasets while maintaining performance on previous segments. The method was tested using a public dataset from the Multiple Sclerosis Segmentation Challenge and an in-house dataset from another hospital, demonstrating improved results compared to training from scratch or using a fixed reference model. This approach was successful in segmenting lesions that were similar to training data, as well as in cross-domain settings with varying levels of training data availability.

A novel concept called dual comparison is presented, which involves comparing two entities by their relationships with a third entity. Different dual comparison methods yield diverse comparison principles and numerous applications. The entity for comparison serves as an intermediary to establish comparisons, and its properties are thus crucial. For the purpose of theoretical analysis, a specific comparison class, denoted as $\mathcal{I}_d$, is introduced, which will aid in proving essential theorems related to dual comparison. By drawing upon the properties of dual comparison, a method to measure entropy of arbitrary Markov processes is developed using the maximum mutual information principle. This approach to entropy measurement has numerous practical implications and showcases the potential of dual comparison. Various comparison methods of Markov processes are presented, along with their relationships. A notable example of dual comparison is the comparison of random matrices based on their non-diagonal elements' expected values. A comprehensive analysis of different dual comparison methods to this specific entity is provided. Additionally, a novel comparison principle for stationary homogeneous Markov processes is presented, along with its related applications. The presented ideas and methods provide a clear understanding of how dual comparison can be applied to solve problems. To demonstrate the practicality of dual comparison, several real-world examples are provided. The provided examples illustrate the effectiveness of dual comparison.

Artificial intelligence systems are increasingly applying their knowledge to real-world problems without fully understanding their own limitations. In many instances, these limitations arise from inaccuracies in their initial constitution. It has been discovered that models based on ordinary differential equations, which account for their own predictive errors, show reduced inaccuracies when put through various scenarios including incomplete data collection and dynamic changes in their environment. This research explores the concept of incorporating model mistakes in ODE models through a metric measuring their deviation from correct solutions. This analysis provides specific boundaries on predictive errors committed by these incomplete models. It has been found that local approximations of ODE models with incorporated errors provide little to no reduction in inaccuracies. It has been observed that the most effective models accounting for their own mistakes are linear models and universal approximation schemes. It has been noted that non-linear models accounting for their own mistakes may not provide any benefits in real-world applications of prediction. It has been found that the addition of error models in combination with available data can both lower and upper bound their respective inaccuracies. It has been noted that the approaches of inference and representation sharing in model error incorporation have different implications on their respective inaccuracies. This research also proposes a framework for designing machine learning methods that incorporate initial model mistakes in ODE models. It has been found from practical applications of this framework that the addition of error models in linear gasification models results in significant reductions of errors by as much as 50%.

The evolution of molecular cloud cores and their relationship with the formation of massive stars remains a critical area of research, particularly regarding the development of cores and the time required for massive star formation to occur. Researchers have been conducting a comprehensive study of the Dragon complex, a nearby star-formding region located at 250 parsecs, using the IRAM 30-m telescope to observe CO (2-1) emission. Their analysis involved a 12-point survey of the complex. The data showed that the main CO emission comes from a 1.5 parsec radius and 10 parsec radius areas. The cores within the complex exhibit velocities ranging from -10 to -4 km/s. The researchers found that the cores within the complex exhibit size reductions as they get denser. The centers of the cores show high velocity dispersion, indicating their transition to heated cores. Their analysis suggests that the cores within the Dragon complex still have time to form massive stars. The project's high-density cores have not yet developed into the protostellar stage, but the presence of high-density hot cores indicates they are close to initiating the protostellar phase.

PopSyCLE is an initial conditions generator designed for cosmological simulations, offering flexibility in the generation of dark matter halos. The code can be used to simulate various types of matter, including the dark matter necessary for simulating the effects of Primordial Black Holes on dark matter halos. We present three sets of PBH dark matter initial conditions for PopSyCLE that differ in their assumptions regarding PBH seeding and dark matter heating. These initial conditions can be used in N-body simulations to be combined with post-processing techniques, such as subhalo identification and PBH heating of dark matter halos.

A simplified model involving a chain of rigid wedges, formed by balls, interacting with an Einstein crystal, has been created and analyzed. This model satisfies two key conditions that distinguish it from other models: (i) the geometric constraint where each site consists of a single ball, and (ii) the Newtonian interaction between balls, which only considers short-range potentials between adjacent sites. These unique conditions give rise to a dynamic behavior where splay order forms in a series of distinct stages influenced by the external temperature. Notably, three distinct regimes can be observed: an Arrhenius stage where the movement of the chain is relatively straightforward; a stage where the formation of permanent defects occurs and exhibits temperature-dependent behavior; and a stage where the formation of these defects is reduced and the chain behaves in a disorder-like manner, which is characterized by a linear relationship between the energy and entropy, similar to the equation of state of a Lennard-Jones gas.

To achieve the best results in the context of parameter-efficient language models, 
it's crucial to adjust the unique token embeddings associated with a given task or batch.
This study focuses on developing a simple and effective method for adjusting unique token embeddings in 
a more efficient way, which does not require the entire model to be fine-tuned.
Our analysis of this approach demonstrates that it has superior performance and is more computationally efficient.
This method also facilitates easier analysis and understanding of the process, as well as serving as a baseline comparison for other adjustments methods.
We tested and validated our method by adjusting unique token embeddings for MoCo denoising objectives in several scenarios, 
which resulted in consistent and significant improvements across different cases.

The study of preference lists, a fundamental subject in mathematics and economics, has garnered interest from various researchers. The Additive Preference Ordering (APO) theory, a category of complete partial orders, provides an alternative to traditional scalar valuations. APO can be viewed as a generalization of the real numbers, where elements are assigned additive preferences. This study explores the creation of APOs from alternative numerical value representations, one being context-free and the other being non-contextual. It is demonstrated that context-free and non-non-contextual APOs are distinct concepts. An application of conditional preference models in a multi-agent auction setting is also presented, showcasing their capability to accommodate complex agent interactions. This work develops a framework for comparing conditional numerical values to partial orders, specifically addressing the problem of set addition for transitive preference orderings, and provides an algorithm for solving this issue. The study experimentally evaluates various machine learning approaches for creating additive preference orderings from numerical value representations and discusses their practical applications in multi-agent auction systems.

Using simulation models, we investigate relationships between heat, mechanical work, and internal vibrations in glass-forming polymer liquids. We focus on the thermal changes resulting from mechanical stimuli, as well as the internal vibrations triggered by such changes. Furthermore, we investigate the connections between internal vibrations, internal energy, and configurational changes in the system. Our findings indicate that a specific thermal dissipation mechanism underpinning the structural changes in these liquids is also applicable to their internal vibrations and configurational changes, with the latter's characteristics tied to the variations of the liquid's components. This discovery enables a deeper understanding of the interplay between heat, mechanical work, and internal energies in glass-forming liquids.

This research investigates how the Transformer language model processes denial sentences in response to statements requiring specific categories of information. Since denial is typically used to contradict statements made about particular aspects of a situation, we examine whether the Transformer model can identify the relevant area denied and how it handles that information. Our analysis across various categories indicates that the Transformer model often struggles to adapt to denial contexts and may rely on heuristics such as overemphasizing word "no" in sentence generation. We found that the model's performance in these situations can be enhanced by either altering the input or processing the denial context in a more nuanced manner that considers the underlying information structure.

To optimize production workflows in the form of Not-for-Publication reports generated by machine translation, a tailored module called the Look-forward Attention Module (LAM) has been developed and implemented after the encoder-decoder structure of the Transformer model. This module focuses on accurately translating specific phrases within NFPs that may cause comprehension difficulties due to their unique structure and content. During regular sentences, LAM directs its focus on preceding words, but unlike regular sentences, LAM enables a unique focus on content within NFPs by allowing attention to be allocated to arbitrary positions within the content, and also enables focusing on future words within regular sentences to facilitate understanding of context. Experimental results indicate that LAM improves the accuracy of machine translation for NFPs by up to 3.5 percentage points, and also results in more accurate translations of regular sentences by upholding native speaker standards.

We have explicitly computed the Kontsevich weights for the graphs associated with links and curvatures under various symplectic Poisson structures, revealing a common structure behind their formulas which can be expressed using iterated integrals based on the original form of the symplectic structure. We have provided concrete examples of how these weights can be applied to specific symplectic structures, such as the standard structure on $\mathbb{R}^2$ and the rotation inspired structure on $T^*SO(3)$. Additionally, we have outlined the general procedure for translating the graph weights from one symplectic structure to another.

The study revealed that thermal entropy is not a unique measure of entanglement entropy due to a complex relationship involving a specific interaction term and radius of the entanglement region. Depending on whether the interaction term increases or decreases with radius, thermal entropy either surpasses or is surpassed by entanglement entropy. This observation led to two potential consequences: a possible connection between gravity and lattice models, or a possible anomaly in a specific entropy boundary established by the gravity-entropy conjecture. A related conjecture regarding the relationship between renormalized entanglement entropy and the interaction term was also proposed. The results were achieved through a large N calculation involving a specific sum of conformal field theory parameters, or central charges. The study also highlighted the role of c-bar terms in influencing thermodynamic properties and c-bar terms in large N calculations. The results were further validated by applying numerical methods to calculate thermal and renormalized entanglement entropies, or S_therm and E_R, at various interaction strengths and radii. The study also showed that entropy values can be positive or negative. The option in question is defined by the average of a sequence of independent and identically distributed random variables. The underlying model proposed by Banouillieu consists of a Black-Scholes type equation with some distinct features and a closed-form valuation model based on a two-point quadrature technique. The purpose of this study is to demonstrate that the option price obtained from Banouillieu's method actually corresponds to a specific type of dynamic hedging strategy, which can be achieved through a two-point quadrature technique. Our current understanding places a limit on the gamma-ray flux produced by galaxy clusters and arcs. The estimate is based on observations from the Fermi Large Area Telescope (FERMI-FGS) and relies on a model that accounts for synchrotron radiation, Inverse Compton radiation, and gamma-ray emission from relativistic electrons and cosmic rays. We found that FERMI-FGS places a constraint on the cosmic ray energy density in galaxy clusters and arcs, specifically, u_CR, < 1.4 x 10^-16 erg/cm^3 (at 95% confidence), and this result is comparable to other independent measurements. The data also suggest that galaxy clusters and arcs arcs are a major contributor to the extragalactic gamma-ray background, specifically, 0.13 < B_G/G < 0.35 (at 95%), where B_G is the gamma-ray flux density and G is the area of galaxy clusters and arcs per steradian. The expected signal in future SKA observations would be, 4 x 10^-17 erg/cm^2, and this could be further increased to, 10^-15 erg/cm^2, if the cosmic ray energy density in galaxy clusters and arcs is at or near its limit with available technology to detect the emission from magnetic fields.

A novel theory called Primal Features has made significant advancements, offering a data-driven approach to feature engineering for time-series data, surpassing the limitations of conventional methods like BICEP/Planck problem-prone features in handling synthetic features. This paper explores the potential of detecting the primordial features proposed in Primal Features through the cosmological collider observable in the future surveys such as Cosmic Origins, Gravitational Origin, and other galaxy surveys beyond Planck, showing that the features caused by particle collisions in the early universe might be within the detectable range of the Cosmic Origins survey, a future CMB mission.

A crucial goal of computer vision is to develop models that learn to generalize well across tasks, although achieving this goal remains a challenging task due to the complex interplay between visual features. To tackle this issue, previous studies focused on extracting and visualizing key features from deep convolutional neural networks (CNNs) by applying various visualization techniques, such as gradient-based methods and surrogate models. Nevertheless, to effectively uncover the underlying generalization mechanism in CNNs, it is necessary to discover and analyze the specific components, such as connections and data patterns, that contribute to this mechanism. Therefore, this study aims to develop a novel surrogate model that can identify and analyze the hidden structures within CNNs by leveraging the relationships between the network's weights and input data. To this end, a new attention mechanism is proposed that can effectively capture the interactions between semantic concepts within the input data, such as classes and local objects, based on the network's understanding. By integrating this attention mechanism into a surrogate model, it is possible to identify and analyze the specific sub-patterns at multiple semantic levels, such as object classes, individual objects, and local regions, that contribute to the network's decision-making process, while also highlighting the most relevant data patterns that enable generalization in CNNs. Furthermore, the proposed approach is applied to different CNN architectures, including state-of-the-art transformers, to effectively elucidate their internal structures and latent mechanisms.

Research suggests that a quantum mechanism known as long-range electron-phonon interaction plays a significant role in the pairing of electrons in one-dimensional materials. To explore this concept further, a theoretical study examined the interaction between two electrons in a copper-oxide chain under tension. The results showed that this interaction results in a strong attraction between electrons, mediated by phonons. The data indicated that the magnitude of this interaction increases exponentially with distance. The researchers compared their findings to experimental data obtained from XPS studies, which demonstrated an increase in binding energy with distance in the copper-oxide chains of questionably synthesized and treated 1D samples. The study also identified which specific phonons facilitate this interaction and determined that this particular mechanism is likely the primary driving force behind electron pairing in one-dimensional copper-oxide materials.

To ensure the security of health information, protecting individual health data plays a crucial role. This study takes the MPHIA individual dataset as the focus, which contains 114 subjects' detailed health information. First, the causal structural operators are identified and integrated into the knowledge graph structure of the MPHIA dataset. Subsequently, the causal effects of interventions on knowledge graph nodes are calculated. Interventions were implemented in the dataset, and the causal effects were estimated using two advanced algorithms: Alg 1 and Alg 2. These algorithms were applied to the graph, and their results were compared. Finally, the effects of interventions on the graph nodes were quantified, and the findings indicate that Alg 2 yields more accurate estimates. To validate the feasibility of the approach, the results of both algorithms were evaluated in terms of mean absolute deviation and significance level at 95%. The experiment demonstrates the application of causal structural analysis to the MPHIA individual dataset, which may aid in the development of new interventions for graph nodes to applications in health information systems.

In a study of the chiral magnet Co$_9$Zn$_9$Mn$_2$, researchers found that the transition from the quaternary alloy's metastable phase to its stable phase is characterized by an gradual transition from quasiperfect skyrmion lattice arrays to a uniform magnetization state, rather than an abrupt phase shift, as observed through temperature-dependent small-angle neutron scattering and neutron microscopy. This gradual phase shift is attributed to a phenomenon where the breakdown of the skyrmion lattice array initiates through the introduction of magnetization defects, rather than an abrupt phase transition driven by pinning instabilities. This phenomenon, where the stable phase forms through geometric melting of the metastable phase, is an exception to the established theory of metastable phase transitions and provides insight into the mechanisms governing the metastable phase transitions in magnetic systems.

Introduction:
High-dimensional time-series data from numerous sources are being produced at an increasing rate. Statistical and machine learning approaches are required to analyze this vast amount of information effectively, leading to a high-dimensional dynamic influence model that utilizes a high-dimensional feature space over time to measure the impact of variables on each other. This work presents an in-depth review of the methods developed for processing high-dimensional time-series data, focusing on those involving dynamic networks, state-space models, and point processes. The review aims to provide an extensive overview of the techniques, their differences, and comparisons, revealing gaps in research, particularly the underdevelopment of methods for discrete and symbolic data, temporal network analysis, and graph-based methods. Furthermore, important tools and future research areas are discussed, including graph-based influence models, novel high-dimensional data types, influence network estimation, state-space models, time-series data analysis, variational autoencoders, and wavefunction influence models.

Discussion:
High-dimensional time-series data analysis is an essential area with numerous applications, including the COVID-19 pandemic, neurological disorders, climate research, audio and video detection, and other fields. However, current methods have limitations, such as the availability of model-based techniques for processing general, discrete, and symbolic data as opposed to numerical data. The concept of stable set balance has been explored through the application of an alternate definition rooted in the idea of partitioning. To address the computational challenge posed by excessive calculations, a stable point method has been developed for solving the balance problem in large systems. However, determining the existence of a stable point relies on the evaluation of a binary parameter. When the parameter is positive, a stable point exists, whereas a negative parameter indicates the absence of such a point. Establishing the value of the parameter requires the determination of a maximum stable set size, a computational task that itself is equivalent to the balance problem under investigation. As an alternative, an outside estimation called the maximum stable set radius can be used, allowing for a broader range of potential maximum stable sets to be considered. By utilizing the estimated radius, a balance solution can be found that is close to the optimal stable set size, even if an exact solution cannot be identified. Moreover, balancing factors can be used to refine estimates and achieve an accurate balance, provided that a balance solution exists. These approaches have been successfully applied to real-world datasets, such as ER, BA, planar, and musical networks, demonstrating a significant relationship between graph characteristics and the size of the largest stable set. Furthermore, detailed computational results have been obtained to illustrate the time complexity scale separation that is characteristic of this method.

We develop an innovative technique for hiding visual objects in natural images in high-resolution formats, building upon the reversible data concealment framework. A sophisticated Bayesian Neural Network architecture is designed to accurately decode protected data as well as remove inserted artifacts and reverse the transformation effects from a given decoder. To enhance the quality of the restored images and the precision of the decoding process, we employ a training procedure where we train multiple networks simultaneously. Through extensive experimentation and comparison with the current state-of-the-art methods, our approach demonstrates superior performance in terms of restoring quality, decoding accuracy, and encoding efficiency.

Theoretical dynamo theories have made significant progress in recent years, with the development of complex mean-field frameworks that capture a broad spectrum of turbulent effects in the latest versions. However, previous studies relying on these frameworks have been limited by only considering a few prominent effects, such as the $\alpha$-emission and diffusion of magnetic fields, in simulations of convective dynamos. To test whether these frameworks can accurately represent more subtle turbulent influences, a study used a realistic 3D convective dynamo simulation to compare with mean-field models incorporating a fuller range of these effects. The results show that including additional subtle turbulent influences in the framework can significantly improve the match with the full 3D simulation, revealing complex and nonlinear interactions between these effects that can vary depending on factors like the strength of convective forcing and the geometry of the system.

Using the ALMA, we have discovered a massive molecular outflow in NGC4945, a 4-kiloparsec wide, 140-kiloparsec long feature that is home to high-velocity gas. Our observations reveal how this outflow was produced, with the most violent activity happening at the very center. We observed different gas speeds but no distinct separation, indicating that the outflow has not changed much since it was produced. Our models show that the outflow is mostly responsible for NGC4945's emission. Using our data, we were able to calculate the mass of the outflow and its kinetic energy. We found that the outflow is massive and highly energetic. We also found that the outflow is driven by the radio jet that powers the central star formation, although the exact mechanism is still unknown. Our research indicates that the outflow's energy is much higher than what the galaxy can produce naturally. It suggests that the outflow may be much larger than we initially thought and could be hundreds of kiloparsecs wide. Our research indicates that the outflow continues to transport gas at high speeds. A numerical method for the quasilinear diffusion model in magnetized plasmas has been developed using the Galerkin method. By constructing the discrete flux as a convex combination of linear diffusion and upwind inviscid fluxes, a conservative and monotonic-increment scheme was obtained. In contrast to previous work, this approach generalizes to comprehensive quasilinear models, encompassing both electric and magnetic drifts without distinction. Furthermore, a flexible framework is established, allowing for the use of various microinstabilities without explicitly accounting for their specific characteristics. Instead, their effects are incorporated into the respective tunnelling parameters, applied consistently across the plasma volume. In addition to theoretical derivation, essential aspects of the method implementation and numerical simulation are explored through illustrative examples.

Previous variable stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods have already been implemented using the Nordsieck technique, and we extend this work by directly introducing variable stepsize SGLMs onto non-uniform grids. We then establish order conditions for these new methods with non-uniform stepsize Second Derivative General Linear Methods (SGLMs), and prove that a specific variable stepsize implementation satisfies the theoretical conditions it's based on. Moreover, we test the new methods on several non-stiff problems to showcase their efficiency, comparing them to existing variable stepsize Runge-Kutta methods.

This study delves into the exponential stability of abounded c0-semigroup in a Banach space and its robustness with respect to perturbations. More specifically, it presents a condition based on Lyapunov theory in the A0-convexity set framework that ensures the preservation of exponential stability under perturbations. Distinguishing this approach is the substitution of the classical energy estimate with the Lyapunov function in the robustness theory of semigroups.

This paper introduces MuMuPy, a computational software for determining how dimuonium binds with substances in electronic atomic form. The program takes into account the dynamic interaction between the bound states of two muons and the surrounding atoms of the substance, utilizing the finite field method to address relativistic effects. Its Relativistic Variational Perturbation Theory framework enables the computation of accurate energy calculations, including spectral data and charge distributions. MuMuPy currently supports calculations for water, methanol, and formamide in their ground states, with further development planned to expand support for various substances and atomic orbitals.

Portfolio managers assess investment success relative to market standards, considering how their returns compare to those of a benchmark index. Besides traditional measures like Sharpe ratio, more sophisticated analysts use a power utility function of return ratios to evaluate performance. This study develops a mathematical model for an investor aiming to maximize the average power utility of both absolute and relative returns. This model introduces a novel dual control approach, allowing us to derive an explicit, optimal portfolio strategy. Its effectiveness is demonstrated through a numerical example.

The possible influence of an galaxy's environment on its evolution has a notable body of theoretical research but lacks sufficient empirical evidence from observational studies in lower-mass galaxies. We present a study that uses a comprehensive analysis of absorption within the Lyman-alpha forest of intergalactic gas to assess environmental effects on the evolution of dwarf galaxies. Through simulations of N-body and smooth particle hydrodynamics, we generated a dataset that informs our selection of absorption spectrum criteria, and found that strong absorption lines in a galaxy's spectrum generally originate from outflows rather than redshifted background quasars. These outflows have average recession velocities of approximately 200 km/s. We discovered that strong absorption within a given recession velocity range correlates with the galaxy's total mass, and our analysis suggests a nonlinear relationship between galaxy mass and the magnitude of this absorption. Compared to our predicted model, we observed a roughly 30% discrepancy in strong absorption at the low-mass range. However, our findings imply that gas within a galaxy's vicinity may play a more significant role in its evolution than previously thought, and may explain observed discrepancies between simulated and observed galaxy properties in this mass range.

The phenomenon of particle upon particle (pupP) has been examined in a context where it is influenced by local bosons and competing effects. It's particularly noteworthy that the presence of bosons leads to an unusual disappearance of fermionic quasiparticles at low quasiparticle densities and low boson concentrations, resulting in a sign of marginal stability. Furthermore, the model generates an inherently unstable quasiparticle in the absence of bosons, while its disappearance gives rise to an additional marginally stable mode. When considering the impact of boson loss on quasiparticles, it's found that the latter can potentially become unstable when exposed to sufficiently intense boson flux, even in the absence of boson gain. Additionally, some key characteristics of theupP phenomenon are shared by systems that exhibit Cooper pair and triplet superfluids, as well as by systems that exhibit competing effects in the absence of a magnetic field. Lastly, some key characteristics of theupP phenomenon are shared by systems that exhibit competing effects in the absence of a magnetic field and systems that exhibit unconventional responses to the onset of superfluidity.

The Thompson's groups T, T2, and T2^2, as well as their braided counterparts F, F2, and F2^2, are geometric groups that have been studied extensively. Notably, they have infinite dimension, but their growth rates are known. Research by Brown and Nekrashevych demonstrated a connection to rooted trees and incisions, enabling a characterization of their growth rates through root dimensions. This work builds upon theirs to investigate the divergence characteristics of these groups. Divergence characteristics compensate the growth rates in various contexts and have been well-studied in finite and locally finite groups. In the case of the Thompson's groups, their growth rates are also infinite, but their divergence characteristics become finite. This paper provides a characterization of the divergence characteristics of T, T2, and T2^2 through tree height and branching number, mirroring Brown and Nekrashevych's findings. It also shows that the same analysis applies to the braided Thompson's groups. Notably, these groups exhibit the property that their growth rates are equal to the square of their divergence characteristics multiplied by 4. The authors also investigate the subgroups of T and T2 that have finite divergence characteristics, as well as the isometries of their Cayley graphs. Additionally, this work explores the presentations of these groups using generators and relations. In particular, the group T2 admits many such presentations, which Brown had identified as 'best'. This paper explores the application of the Complete RAG framework for question answering tasks. Although RAG models its own queries as questions and retrieves relevant answers from long texts, it faces a problem with unanswerable queries. To resolve this issue, this work examines under what conditions the distributions of retrievable answers and non-retrievable answers from the same long text overlap. A modified loss is proposed during pre-training to increase the model's confidence in unanswerable queries with no retrieved data. Additionally, this loss is also tested in a ranking task to improve the model's ability to retrieve relevant answers. A dataset specifically designed for this task has been created with points of interest from Wikipedia, Instruct2Vec, and Geotag datasets. Our results indicate that the proposed loss enhances both pre-training and fine-tuning performance for question answering tasks.

This study calculates the long-term behavior of the recurrence coefficients for polynomials that are orthogonal in relation to a logarithmic weight given by $\log\frac{1+\epsilon f(x)}{1+\epsilon}$. It specifically analyzes the behavior of the coefficients as the size of the polynomials approaches infinity. The analysis involves the use of two vector bundles over a manifold with corners, where one of the boundaries has a specific type of singularity, to represent a family of monic orthogonal polynomials that depends on $f$ and $\epsilon$. The Calogero-Moser equation and its connection to a Lax pair provide crucial algebraic tools for this calculation. The derived asymptotic formula for the coefficients is expressed through a connection between the coefficients and Chern forms of the two vector bundles, which simplifies the expression and reveals a universal constant that does not depend on $f$. This constant is a specific value of the Chern form on a circle at the singular boundary. The calculation is made possible by an extension of techniques from [A. Pushnitsky, J. Math. Phys. 57(21), 212797 (2016)], which applies to a compact manifold, and by a generalization of the methods to a manifold with a singular boundary.

Developing automated text summarization models is a daunting task, requiring a substantial task workforce that possesses exceptional language skills, domain expertise, and is motivated to contribute.  Unfortunately, such a workforce does not exist.  In order to improve performance and achieve state-of-the-art results, we conducted a comprehensive analysis of various MTurk settings aimed at identifying and recruiting high-quality workers.  Through an extensive evaluation involving 591 unique workers across 31 experiments, we investigated the effectiveness of individual and joint qualifications, including rewriting tasks, testing knowledge, language proficiency, consistency, and reliability.  In this paper, we report on our findings, present the qualification structures of the best-performing models, and demonstrate how to leverage worker qualifications to design more effective retrieval algorithms, resulting in models that surpass the state-of-the-art performance on the Gigaword and NewsDiscourse datasets.

Text-video retrieval, an essential task of practical importance, has seen escalating interest, with the focus on crafting nuanced spatial-temporal video representations being a major research priority. Current state-of-the-art models for text-video retrieval heavily rely on sophisticated yet computationally expensive image transformers and 3D convolutional networks, limiting their application to be narrow-scope and computationally expensive. This paper presents TS2-Net, a groundbreaking text-video retrieval framework featuring a novel Token Shift and Choice module, achieving high performance while being resource-efficient. With the ability to reach 83.6 mAP on VL-Kinetics-Google for 4-GPU training, TS2-Net has set a new performance standard, with supporting results also available on https://github.com/AlibabaResearch/DAR-OpenMind/tree/main/TS2-Net.

We investigate a theoretical model postulating neutral currents can modify flavour in a manner consistent with the Standard Model's $SU(2)_L \times U(1)_Y$ symmetry. This leads to a hypothetical fourth generation of heavy quarks, facilitating flavour-changing neutral currents. Our analysis focuses on observable signatures in top quark-associated processes at the Large Hadron Collider. These include flavour-dependent CP violation and anomalous flavour combinations in top quarks or W bosons. This novel approach provides signatures distinct from both third generation anomalous neutral couplings and tree-level exotic quark flavours.

In the realm of network science, random networks are frequently studied to uncover their inherent properties. However, when employing the uniform attachment method used by Molloy and Reed in the late 1980s, random networks typically exhibit short cycles and a single dominant hub. The development of the preferential attachment method by Barabasi and coworkers in the early 2000s led to the creation of a new class of random networks characterised by the power law distribution of node degrees. Their approach results in the emergence of a distinct two-phase process, comprising an initial phase dominated by a single hub and a longer second phase characterised by the power law distribution of node degrees. The proposed directed hybrid random network combines the preferential attachment and uniform attachment methods to better model complex phenomena and offers a more versatile and practical approach to degree distribution, allowing for the coexistence of power law degree distributions with smaller or absent hubs, as well as degree distributions that deviate from the power law through the introduction of a non-linear preferential attachment mechanism. The proposed network is found to display a wide range of degree properties and associated temporal evolution patterns. The research demonstrates that the proposed networks effectively capture the observed characteristics of many real-world networks and provide a practical tool for the prediction, simulation, and testing of network dynamics and degree distribution. The coexistence of nodes with degree properties spanning from linear to logarithmic is particularly notable. The expansion of wireless communication systems has significant implications for the environment, particularly when it comes to noise pollution. Effective management of this issue involves developing an advanced network monitoring system that can automatically detect disturbances and identify their specific locations. This requires sophisticated signal processing capabilities, as wireless disturbances can vary in intensity and origin. A Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) approach has been found to be a reliable solution for such a task, especially in areas where data collection and analysis methods are complex and difficult to implement. This paper focuses on multi-label wireless disturbance detection using CNNs, building on existing research in this field. A thorough examination of related concepts, such as noise pollution and the application of deep learning in wireless network management, is provided, along with a review of the current state of the art. A detailed description of the proposed method, involving CNN-based localization of wireless disturbances by analyzing meta-data, is presented, including its implementation and evaluation. Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed method is effective in localizing multiple sources simultaneously.

To investigate the interaction energy of Klein-Gordon particles and a cosmic string, researchers consider a particle dislocated both spatially and temporally. The study focuses on a specific spacetime influenced by a cosmic string and an exponential potential, featuring a position-dependent mass term. The work aims to understand how a cosmic string and particle displacement affect the properties of Klein-Gordon particles, specifically their behavior influenced by the gravitational potential and displacement potential. For practical purposes, the authors calculate the energy of Klein-Gordon particles as a function of various physical parameters. The study reveals that displacement modulates particle behavior in response to the gravitational and potential influences. Furthermore, the researchers observe that discrete displacements of the particle can lead to discontinuous changes in its energy. This effect is more pronounced in scenarios where the gravitational potential is significant. For specific displacement values, the authors find that the relationship between vortex and energy is linear, as well as the relationship between charge and energy. However, these relationships are non-linear for all other considered charge and vortex values.

A nonatomic, locally normal measure algebra $\mathcal{A}$ on a Polish space $X$ is considered. It is demonstrated that the Hausdorff dimension of the unit interval associated with $\mathcal{A}$ can be minimal, yet greater than zero. Specifically, for any real number $s>0$, a Polish space $X$ and a closed subset $Y$ of $X$ can be identified, such that the Hausdorff dimension of $Y$ is less than or equal to $s$, and the unit interval associated with the measure algebra generated by $Y$ has a Hausdorff dimension greater than $s$.

Deep Inelastic Scattering experiments using a nuclear target can identify two distinct electroweak processes. One involves a photon exchange between the proton and the target, while the other is a QCD-mediated interaction between the proton and the target. Although the proton is exposed to a potential alignment in the direction of its recoil due to the electromagnetic field, this characteristic is expected to vanish for unpolarized targets. However, a new observable known as the Recoil Proton Alignment (RPA) emerges when the proton is polarized and impinged upon an unpolarized nuclear target. Calculations suggest that the RPA observable can be quite substantial and may serve as a vital discriminant in isolating the Differential Vector Meson Photoproduction on the proton and DVCS processes.

This research seeks to contribute to the advancement of artificial intelligence by examining its potential to surpass human intelligence. Despite decades of study, achieving this goal remains a pressing challenge. By reviewing the prevailing literature, we isolated key methodologies employed in the vast majority of studies (75%) to 2021. Additionally, we identified primary areas of focus for future studies, all of which can be organized into four core categories. Notably, one primary area of focus, later categorized as 'Sensory Integration,' received only 2% of the studied attention, despite being a crucial aspect. Consequently, this study proposes the concept of 'Enhanced AI' to facilitate a more comprehensive understanding of artificial intelligence systems, encompassing a broader range of methodologies and future directions, including Sensory Integration.

Our research utilizes the density-matrix time-evolving block calculations to study the phase transitions in a bosonic system subjected to a strong optical lattice at low temperatures. The system exhibits a superfluid to supersolid phase transition, and its stability is examined in relation to the strength of the optical lattice and spin-orbit coupling. The results indicate that the supersolid phase exhibits greater resistance to changes in these parameters, and the shifts in phase stability can be accurately predicted based on the system's ground state. Additionally, the system's response to spin-orbit coupling reveals a distinct molecular pattern that persists beyond the critical point, and its impact on the phase transition is significant.

Consider a finite abelian group $G$ and let $V_G$ denote the set of subsets of $G$ having an odd number of elements. A function $\phi_G$ mapping $V_G$ to the set of non-negative integers is defined by $\phi_G (S)$ being the smallest integer dividing the difference of two elements in $S$ of the same parity. The authors of this work propose that the sequence $\{\phi_G (S)\}$ consists of positive integers with a specific distribution, which they then demonstrate for a particular abelian group $G$ by utilizing another function $\omega_G$ mapping the elements of $G$ to the set of prime numbers and establishing upper limits for the number of subsets $S$ of $G$ for which $\phi_G (S) \le k$. The authors also provide two applications, which involve the occurrence of odd periods in pairs of relatively prime arithmetic functions and the upper limits of the number of elements in the set $V_G$ when $|G|$ is large.

We examined the dual quantum field theories on $(1+1)$ and $(2+1)$ dimensions using the holographic AdS/CFT framework, revealing novel observations, initial assumptions in this field, and numerical calculations. This included analyzing solitons in AdS spacetimes. When considering one-dimensional systems, we delved into the physics of classical AdS solitons with a pure gauge supergravity solution and explored self-sustaining mechanisms in systems with a pure Yang-Mills theory dual. Additionally, we conducted thorough investigations in three-dimensional systems, covering classical and weak Yang-Mills theories, classical string solutions with Type IIA theory backgrounds, and an in-depth analysis confirmed that our substantial type IIA solution indeed has a holographic dual. Moreover, we have demonstrated the existence of solutions that mirror low-dimensional systems with negative central charges, thereby capping the cynicism surrounding such concepts as negative $\mathcal{N}$ and $\lambda$.

A Gaussian Process regression model's effectiveness heavily relies on the choice of kernel, which determines the expected similarity between any two points. In this study, we explore kernels based on fundamental mathematical expressions like addition, multiplication, and exponentiation, and their expected behavior is theoretically analyzed. These novel kernels are tested on multiple real-world datasets and shown to perform comparably to the commonly used exponential kernel. Furthermore, we find that modifying the multiplication kernel through data preparation can lead to performance improvements for datasets with inputs that have meaning beyond their labels.

Future muon colliders are expected to be highly susceptible to beam-induced backgrounds. Consequently, effective strategies are needed to manage these effects and reduce noise in collider observations. This paper presents various design-based approaches aimed at minimizing background interference. Data from the LHC provides context for addressing muon collider challenges. Potential strategies for reducing noise include optimizing particle pileup, identifying and isolate beam-generated particles, separating signal from background noise, reducing noise in detector data, and utilizing artificial intelligence algorithms to isolate signal data. Each of these tactics is explored in detail, illustrated with relevant diagrams and examples.

Introducing Spartan, a novel approach for training neural networks with pre-defined sparsity in mind. By leveraging a differentiable sparseness criterion, Spartan makes it possible to exclude a subset of trainable parameters from being updated, thereby allowing the exploration of pre-defined sparsity levels. This is achieved through a straightforward optimization problem with an extensive range of possible sparsity patterns. In comparison to existing methods, Spartan's performance can be seen as flexibly navigating the trade-off between regulization strength and adaptability. This research is the first to demonstrate the effectiveness of using conformal prediction in the context of neural network training, thereby providing a predictive margin of error that could potentially be fine-tuned to achieve higher accuracy.

According to the Bloch theorem, gapped systems in periodic environments exhibit dispersionless surface states, a phenomenon known as the Pauli obstruction. This principle is exemplified by Weyl points in Dirac semimetals and by the protected surface states of topological insulators. However, a notable exception to this principle is observed in strongly interacting many-body systems, where the emergence of non-dispersive, polarized eigenstates along high-dimensional manifolds is facilitated by non-Abelian gauge symmetries derived from spin and other characteristics. In this study, a theory is developed to describe the disappearance of the Pauli obstruction in systems featuring weakly interacting bosons, a scenario influenced by non-interacting dispersion relationships but ultimately determined by strongly interacting many-body dynamics. This investigation identifies specific conditions under which this phenomenon occurs and establishes that strong interactions can trigger a dispersionless eigenstate shift from high-dimensional to high-dimensional manifolds of varying dimensions. This development enables the use of topological invariant analysis to accurately predict the disappearance of the Pauli obstruction, a phenomenon that may be experimentally verified using spectroscopy with high energy and spatial resolution.

The prevalence of smelly code in open-source software is a topic of ongoing debate, with some developers downplaying its incidence and others deeming it widespread. A five-question survey sent to 511 Java developers yielded a 22.8% response rate, with the majority (75.5%) believing smelly code is common and all respondents agreeing it's a significant issue. Notably, the study found that fear of criticism from peers, rather than complexity, appears to hinder open-source contributors from sharing their code, and over 90% of respondents suggested that buddy review mechanisms could effectively address this issue.

The study presents novel existence results for differential-inclusion solutions, employing an iterative sweeping process, thereby relaxing conventional Lipschitz assumptions regarding the mapping that drives the inclusion process. The results achieved encompass both continuous and right-continuous cases. Furthermore, the paper demonstrates the significance of its findings through the derivation of two valuable applications: first, in establishing a right-continuous version of the second-order reparametrization of Filippov systems, and second, in proving the existence of solutions for the inclusion process involving the sliding regulus, thereby addressing the long-standing "problem of sliding regularity."

We introduce several advancements in the KKMCee event generator, specifically for pair production of leptons and quarks in collider experiments: a new Monte Carlo approach, integration links with other generators, precision realizations of pair production processes including heavy neutral Higgs bosons, the neutral Higgs bosons Z' and the pseudoscalar particle X/superaxion and, finally, the creation of heavy neutral Higgs bosons through pair production in conjunction with radiation of W bosons. These advancements are incorporated into the event generator with attention to efficiency, accuracy, performance, and compatibility issues, including interfacing with parameter cards, that enable seamless use of pair production processes. These advancements are evaluated through Monte Carlo statistics and theoretical precision, specifically for pair production of heavy neutral Higgs bosons through weak gauge coupling processes. We present a variety of simulated distributions to illustrate the accuracy and precision of simulated data for different processes at lepton colliders. We present results in tabular form for pair production of Standard Model particles including charged leptons, neutrinos, gauge bosons (W and Z), the gauge boson Z' across a variety of a factors and the pseudoscalar X/superaxion for various factors a. These results are presented for pair production of heavy neutral Higgs bosons under a variety of VBM physics scenarios.

Measuring inter-beat intervals from ECG signals is crucial for assessing cardiac health because changes in IB I can indicate cardiovascular disease before symptoms arise, leading to better prevention and treatment outcomes. Developing an accurate algorithm for IB I measurement is vital, and a deep learning model, specifically the Tiramisu Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), has been successfully applied in this study to achieve minimal average beat-to-beat error rates of 0.16 and 0.18 milliseconds for normal and abnormal ECG signals, respectively. By employing a novel combination of loss functions, the Tiramisu model outperformed traditional approaches, and its ability to capture complex features and detect noise patterns yielded exceptional performance.

The stochastic approach to computing the tensor singular value decomposition (t-SVD) offers an alternative method of analyzing large-scale tensors by leveraging the capabilities of modern hardware for parallel processing. This paper builds upon the existing stochastic methods for analyzing high-order matrices, expanding the concept to three-dimensional tensors and incorporating the matrix square root and matrix power operations. An optional limit on the number of iterations is provided, allowing for more control over the computation time. An illustrative comparison demonstrates the performance of our algorithm for 3D tensors and provides insight into its potential applications. An implementation in the R programming language, along with the associated numericalR package, is also provided.

Real-world networks often exhibit dynamic properties, necessitating the representation and analysis of changing graph structures. The goal of this research is to create a mathematical framework for embedding dynamic graphs in a stable Euclidean space. The proposed method extends a previous algorithm by Adams et al. to handle changes in graph topology over time, utilizing Linear Assignment Programming to optimize embeddings that remain consistent across successive time steps. The embedding's stability is measured by the rotation angle. Experimental evaluations on both artificial and real-world networks demonstrate the performance of this method. Notably, the technique has been successfully applied in analyzing the German Power Grid.

In order to locate the ground state of $^7$H, which has two neutrons and five protons, researchers examine $^3$H, which has three protons and one neutron, to determine that it too has a ground state that is stable and distinct from other excited states. Utilizing the $^3$H ground state as a reference point, standard quantum number calculations and hyperspherical harmonic analyses are conducted to identify the ground state of $^7$H at specific couplings within the $fs$ range. It's found that at this range of couplings, the $^7$H ground state is three times the energy of the $^3$H ground state. This $^7$H ground state is also three times the energy of the $^3$H+4n three-body limit. It's noted that the energy of the five protons and two neutrons is approximately zero in the $^7$H system. Furthermore, the study concludes that the $^7$H ground state does not undergo a transition into a clustered $^3$H+4n system at any point within the $fs$ to $D^*$ range of couplings. This work also explores the point where the $^7$H ground state undergoes a transition into a fragmented $^3$H+4n system. To achieve this, the study utilizes the Fock Tamm model. Reiterating a query about a renowned unsolved problem in Riemannian geometry, Nirenberg inquired about the possibility of embedding strictly positively curved manifolds into other, positively curved manifolds of the same dimension. This question has been successfully addressed in certain lower dimensional cases, but the question remains unanswered in higher dimensions. In this talk, we'll present findings concerning the extension of positive functions defined on upper half spheres from their tangent spaces to their ambient space. This investigation encompasses various curvature cases including positive, zero, and negative curvatures. Additionally, we'll demonstrate that the most straightforward method of extending functions, such as linearly, is not possible when curvatures are negative. Finally, we'll demonstrate that the most straightforward method of extending functions, such as padding with a reference value, is both necessary and sufficient for negative curvatures.

A new class of neural optimizers, known as Schur optimizer and generalized Krasnoselski optimizer, has been developed and tested in the context of training deep networks for both binary and multi-label classification tasks. While the conventional Stochastic Gradient Descent method ensures convergence to the global optimal solution when the loss function is consistent with the data distribution, our alternative approach achieves a faster convergence rate for a specific non-random loss function with a larger step-size value. Building on the theoretical framework of neural network training, we demonstrate that our optimizer produces a representation that is optimal in a specific statistical sense, and further derive that the score distributions generated by the optimizer converge to Gaussian mixtures, providing an objective criterion for evaluating the quality of a neural network representation. Furthermore, our experiments validate that the Schur optimizer yields better representations, as measured by the distance between the predicted score distributions and their empirical estimates, resulting in lower generalization errors for multiple benchmark datasets.

In England, a detailed COVID-19 contact tracing program was launched in late 2020. The program's core features included a national system for tracking suspected cases and their contacts. Although widely adopted, questions remained regarding the optimal strategy for excising and tracing contacts. To shed light on this, researchers analyzed the program's performance in Liverpool, where a unique approach to tracing suspected cases and their contacts was taken from mid-August to mid-October 2020. Instead of utilizing the national system, local health officials exercised more aggressive control over extracting and tracing contacts. A time-series analysis was conducted to compare the growth rates of new cases in Liverpool with those in other parts of England. The findings suggested that this different approach resulted in a slight decline in new cases in Liverpool but, compared to other cities in the country, was met with an increased speed in identifying suspected cases. Consequently, the data implies that more aggressive contact tracing can accelerate case resolution without negatively affecting overall outcomes.

Determining the fundamental parameters of star clusters is a vital component of astrophysical research. Utilizing the Gaia DR2 survey provides an opportunity to enhance existing estimates of distances, ages, and star masses based on precise parallax measurements. This study presents a comprehensive analysis of the Melotte 72 star cluster's fundamental properties. By only selecting clusters members with high accuracy parallax values from Gaia DR2, we constructed a color-magnitude diagram. This allowed us to calculate the cluster's age, which we found to be approximately 600 million years, and its visual extinction based on different spectral types. Using the Crowther method for early spectral types and the Pickering method for late spectral types, we calculated the extinction levels across the H-R diagram. Melotte 72's photometric spectral types and mass range were also determined and compared with previous surveys. This study found the cluster's hipparcos estimated parallax to be higher than the Gaia DR2 value, indicating a possible revision of its distance estimate. Additionally, the cluster's Gaia DR2 parallax supports a revised distance range of 2000-2400 parsecs, and its membership flags revealed a small number of likely non-cluster members. This study found the cluster's parallax dispersion to be lower than the hipparcos estimated value, and its binary fraction to be less than 0.3, with a possible presence of blue stragglers.
